# Saturday vs. Sunday: How History Shifted the Sabbath Day of Rest

URL: https://shekinahsda.org/blog/history-of-the-sabbath-change-saturday-to-sunday/
Category: Bible Answers
Author: Caleb Turner
Published: 2026-11-02

The move from Saturday to Sunday took centuries, and this study traces it through the original sources, from Creation and the apostles to Constantine, Laodicea, and the Reformation.


Your teenager comes home from a world history class and asks a simple question over dinner. If the Ten Commandments name the seventh day, why do most churches meet on the first? You start to answer, then realize you are not sure. Later that night you look up the history of the sabbath change from saturday to sunday, and the results argue with each other: one blames an emperor, another credits the apostles, and a third points to a pope.

That confusion is understandable, because each of those answers holds a piece of the story and none of them holds all of it. It unfolded across several centuries, in different cities, for different reasons, and the people involved left writings we can still read. Some of what circulates online about those writings is accurate, and some of it is garbled.

So this article does one thing. It walks through the record in order, from Creation to the Reformation, and lets the sources speak in their own words. Where a text is unclear, we will say so, and where Christians read the evidence differently, we will describe their views fairly. Like the people of Berea, who "searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so" (Acts 17:11, KJV), you are invited to check everything here for yourself.

## The short answer

The shift from Saturday to Sunday was gradual, and no single person made it. Christians were meeting on Sunday by the middle of the second century, as Justin Martyr records. Constantine's law of AD 321 then gave Sunday civil rest, and the Council of Laodicea later pressed believers to work on the Sabbath. Scripture records no such change, so the seventh day remains the Sabbath of the fourth commandment.

That last sentence is a conclusion drawn from reading the Bible, and many sincere Christians reach a different one. The historical facts themselves are shared ground, though. Few who have studied the sources think one emperor flipped a switch, and few claim the New Testament contains a direct command to move the day. What people disagree about is what the slow change means.

- 7th : Day named in the fourth commandment
- Mid 100s : Justin describes the Sunday assembly
- AD 321 : Constantine orders rest on the day of the Sun

## Where does the Sabbath story begin?

The Sabbath begins in the first pages of the Bible, not at Mount Sinai. Genesis says that after the sixth day of Creation God rested, and then it adds: "And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it: because that in it he had rested from all his work which God created and made" (Genesis 2:3, KJV). When the Ten Commandments were given, the fourth one pointed straight back to that moment. It says, "But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God" (Exodus 20:10, KJV), and it gives Creation as the reason.

For the history that follows, one detail matters a great deal. The commandment does not only ask for a weekly rest. It names a particular day and ties it to something God did. That is why the later change is such an interesting question, and why people on every side of it have felt the need to explain it.

## Did Jesus and the apostles change the Sabbath?

The New Testament does not record Jesus or the apostles changing the Sabbath to another day. Luke says Jesus went to the synagogue at Nazareth on the Sabbath "as his custom was" (Luke 4:16, KJV). Jesus disputed how the day was kept, but He defended it rather than removing it, saying, "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath" (Mark 2:27, KJV). After the crucifixion, Luke notes that the women who followed Him "rested the sabbath day according to the commandment" (Luke 23:56, KJV), and Luke wrote those words years after the resurrection.

The book of Acts shows the same day in use across the Roman world. Paul entered the synagogue at Thessalonica "as his manner was" and "three sabbath days reasoned with them out of the scriptures" (Acts 17:2, KJV). At Antioch in Pisidia, Gentiles asked to hear more, and "the next sabbath day came almost the whole city together to hear the word of God" (Acts 13:44, KJV). Many Christians reply, reasonably, that Paul went to synagogues on the Sabbath because that was where he could find an audience. That is a fair point, and these verses alone do not settle the question.

### What about the first day of the week in the New Testament?

The New Testament mentions the first day of the week a handful of times, but no passage says the Sabbath moved to it. Paul met with believers at Troas "upon the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread" (Acts 20:7, KJV), and he told the Corinthians to set money aside on "the first day of the week" (1 Corinthians 16:2, KJV). John also wrote, "I was in the Spirit on the Lord's day" (Revelation 1:10, KJV), without saying which day he meant. Many Christians see in these verses the seeds of Sunday worship, and this article reads them differently.

Those passages deserve careful study of their own, which is why we treat them in a separate article rather than here. For the purposes of history, one observation is worth holding on to. Acts records a sharp public dispute over whether Gentile believers must be circumcised, yet it records no dispute at all about a change of the weekly day. That is an argument from silence, so it should be held with some modesty, but it does suggest that no such change was being pressed in those years.

Related: [Why Worship on Saturday?](https://shekinahsda.org/blog/why-do-seventh-day-adventists-worship-on-saturday/)

## What do we know about the Sabbath in the early church?

The evidence from the first decades after the apostles is thin, and honesty requires saying so. A Roman governor, Pliny the Younger, reported around AD 112 that Christians met "on a fixed day before dawn" (Letters 10.96), but he does not say which day. An early church manual called the Didache, whose date is debated though many scholars place it in the first century, tells believers, "But every Lord's day gather yourselves together, and break bread." Even there the Greek is unusual, and the word "day" has been supplied by the translator, so scholars discuss what the phrase originally meant.

### What did Ignatius and Barnabas say?

Ignatius of Antioch and the letter of Barnabas are two of the earliest writers usually cited, and neither is as simple as the slogans suggest. In the standard English translation, Ignatius describes believers as "no longer observing the Sabbath, but living in the observance of the Lord's Day" (Magnesians 9). The trouble is that the word "Day" is not in the main surviving Greek manuscript, which reads more like living according to the Lord's life. Fritz Guy examined the passage in Andrews University Seminary Studies in 1964 and concluded that it is too ambiguous to serve as clear evidence, though other scholars do read it as a reference to Sunday.

The letter of Barnabas, written by an unknown author, is plainer. It treats the present Sabbath as something God does not accept and then says, "we keep the eighth day with joyfulness," calling it "the day also on which Jesus rose again from the dead" (Barnabas 15). This is a real witness to a Christian Sunday observance, and it would be unfair to explain it away. It is also worth noticing that the writer does not say the Sabbath moved to the eighth day. He presents the eighth day as something new, with its own meaning.

### What did Justin Martyr really write?

Justin Martyr, a Christian teacher at Rome, gives the first detailed description of a Christian Sunday service, written around the middle of the second century. In his First Apology, chapter 67, he says, "But Sunday is the day on which we all hold our common assembly," and he describes Scripture reading, teaching, prayer, the bread and wine, and gifts for widows and orphans. He gives two reasons: God began Creation on that day, and Jesus rose on it. This was roughly 170 years before Constantine's law, so anyone who claims that Constantine invented Sunday worship is simply mistaken.

Justin also helps us understand how he thought about the Sabbath, and he is often misread here. He did not teach that the Sabbath had moved to Sunday. In his Dialogue with Trypho he argues that the Sabbath was a sign given to Israel, and that it was no longer needed now that Christ had come. He says, "The new law requires you to keep perpetual sabbath" (chapter 12), meaning a whole life of faithfulness. Yet in chapter 47 he says that a believer in Christ who still keeps the law of Moses "will be saved" if he does not press it on others, and he admits that some Christians refused fellowship with such people. In other words, Sabbath keeping believers were still around in his day, and the church had not reached one mind about them.

### Why did Sunday gain ground?

Scholars give several reasons for the growth of Sunday, and they do not all agree on how the reasons fit together. The reason the early writers themselves give is the resurrection, and that deserves real respect. Christianity Today's Christian History magazine says that no single name or date is attached to the change, that growing numbers of Gentile converts played a part, and that Sunday was the norm by the end of the first century. Samuele Bacchiocchi, a Sabbath keeping scholar writing in Biblical Archaeology Review in 1978, argued for a later date and a different place. He held that the change came "sometime after 135 A.D.," started in Rome rather than Jerusalem, and was spurred by Roman repressive measures after the Jewish revolts.

Both views are held by serious people, and the sources are thin enough that neither can claim the last word. Bacchiocchi's Rome theory has also been challenged, even by another Sabbath keeping scholar. Around AD 200, Tertullian in North Africa shows the practice maturing. He says that on the day of the resurrection Christians should avoid kneeling, "deferring even our businesses" (On Prayer 23), which is an early hint of setting work aside. In his Apology, chapter 16, he also has to answer pagans who assumed that Christians worshiped the sun, and he insists that their joy on that day has a different cause. His same discussion of kneeling notes that "some few" also avoided kneeling on the Sabbath, a small sign that the seventh day still held meaning for some.

## What did Constantine's Sunday law of 321 actually say?

Constantine's law of March 7, 321 ordered city dwellers and workshops to stop work on the day of the Sun, while allowing farmers to continue. Philip Schaff, the church historian, translates its opening this way: "On the venerable Day of the Sun let the magistrates and people residing in cities rest, and let all workshops be closed." The law survives in the Code of Justinian, book 3, title 12, where its Latin phrase is "venerabili die Solis." Elsewhere in the same history, Schaff notes that many church histories leave out the exception for farm work, which was allowed because planting could not always wait.

The wording shows what the law was and what it was not. Schaff writes, "There is no reference whatever in his law either to the fourth commandment or to the resurrection of Christ." It uses the old name for the day, which he suggests could speak to pagan and Christian subjects at once, and he calls Constantine the founder, in part at least, of the civil observance of Sunday. Later that same year another decree allowed slaves to be freed on the day. So Constantine did not create Christian Sunday worship, and he did not abolish the Sabbath. What he did was give an existing Christian custom the weight of Roman law, and that mattered a great deal.

Related: [Did Constantine Really Change the Bible?](https://shekinahsda.org/blog/did-constantine-change-the-bible/)

## What did the Council of Laodicea decide?

The Council of Laodicea was a regional church gathering in the fourth century that told Christians not to rest on the Sabbath. Its exact date is uncertain, and the introduction in the New Advent edition places it somewhere between AD 343 and 381. Canon 29 reads, "Christians must not judaize by resting on the Sabbath, but must work on that day, rather honouring the Lord's Day; and, if they can, resting then as Christians." It closes by declaring that those found to be judaizers are to be "anathema from Christ," which is the language of being cut off.

Two details are often missed, and they make the picture more interesting. First, this canon came from one regional council, not from the whole church, and its Sunday instruction is gentle: rest "if they can." Second, the same council did not treat the Sabbath as an ordinary day. Canon 16 says, "The Gospels are to be read on the Sabbath," and canons 49 and 51 set the Sabbath beside the Lord's Day as the two days for certain observances in Lent. It seems reasonable to conclude that a rule against resting on the Sabbath would not be needed unless some Christians were still doing so, though the canon itself does not tell us how many.

## How long did Christians keep both days?

Many Christians gathered on both days well into the fifth century, according to two historians of that period. Socrates Scholasticus wrote that "almost all churches throughout the world celebrate the sacred mysteries on the sabbath of every week," and he adds that Christians at Alexandria and Rome had stopped doing so "on account of some ancient tradition" (Church History 5.22). His contemporary Sozomen says that the people of Constantinople, "and almost everywhere, assemble together on the Sabbath, as well as on the first day of the week," a custom never observed at Rome or at Alexandria (Church History 7.19). Neither writer says these churches rested from work as the fourth commandment directs, so these reports describe gatherings, not full Sabbath keeping.

Their reports still correct a common picture. The move was not a clean swap in which one day ended and another began. For several hundred years the two days overlapped, with different customs in different regions.

- Creation: God blesses the seventh day: The day is sanctified because God rested on it (Genesis 2:3).

- Sinai: The fourth commandment: The seventh day is named as the Sabbath (Exodus 20:10).

- First century: Jesus and the apostles: Luke and Acts show the Sabbath still in use, with no recorded change.

- About AD 112: Pliny's report: Christians meet on "a fixed day" that he does not name.

- Mid second century: Justin Martyr: The first detailed description of a Sunday assembly.

- March 7, 321: Constantine's law: City rest on the day of the Sun, with farmers exempt.

- AD 343 to 381: Council of Laodicea: Canon 29 tells Christians to work on the Sabbath.

- Fifth century: Socrates and Sozomen: Many churches still gather on both days, but not Rome or Alexandria.

- 1530 and 1646: Protestant confessions: Augsburg and Westminster each explain Sunday in their own way.

## Who changed the Sabbath to Sunday, according to the churches themselves?

Different Christian traditions answer this question differently, and it helps to let each one speak for itself. Thomas Aquinas, the great medieval Catholic teacher, wrote that "the observance of the Lord's day took the place of the observance of the Sabbath, not by virtue of the precept but by the institution of the Church and the custom of Christian people" (Summa Theologiae, Second Part of the Second Part, question 122, article 4). The Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraph 2175, says of Sunday that "for Christians its ceremonial observance replaces that of the sabbath," and it adds, "In Christ's Passover, Sunday fulfills the spiritual truth of the Jewish sabbath." The same paragraph also says that Sunday "is expressly distinguished from the sabbath which it follows chronologically every week," so on the Catechism's own terms the two days remain distinct.

Protestants have not spoken with one voice either. The Augsburg Confession of 1530, a founding Lutheran statement, reports in its public domain English translation that its opponents point to the change as proof of church authority, saying, "Great, say they, is the power of the Church, since it has dispensed with one of the Ten Commandments!" It rejects that argument, teaching instead that the Sabbath has been set aside by Scripture and that "the Church designated the Lord's Day" so people would know when to assemble. The Westminster Confession of the 1640s takes another path, saying that the Sabbath was the last day of the week until the resurrection of Christ, and then "was changed into the first day of the week." So one tradition points to the Church, one to Christian liberty, and one to a change made at the resurrection.

| Source | How it explains Sunday |
| --- | --- |
| Thomas Aquinas | The Lord's Day took the Sabbath's place by Church institution and Christian custom |
| Catechism of the Catholic Church | Sunday replaces the Sabbath's ceremonial observance and fulfills its meaning |
| Augsburg Confession | The Sabbath set aside; the Church chose a day for assembly |
| Westminster Confession | The Sabbath changed to the first day at the resurrection |
| This article's reading | Scripture records no change, so the seventh day remains the Sabbath |

Reading these statements side by side is striking, and it calls for humility rather than point scoring. These are thoughtful Christians trying to be faithful, and they agree on the most important fact about Jesus: He rose from the dead. Yet their different explanations show that the change is not something the Bible states in a single clear sentence. Our reading is that God blessed the seventh day, that Scripture never transfers that blessing, and that the Sabbath still stands, while the resurrection remains the center of our hope on every day of the week.

## How can you weigh this history for yourself?

The best way to weigh this history is to go back to the documents and to read them slowly. Every passage quoted here is short enough to read in one sitting, and most are free online. Start with the Bible, then read Justin, Constantine's law, and Laodicea in that order, and notice who is speaking and when. A family could do this over a few evenings.

Be careful with quotations, too, since this is one topic where a striking line can travel a long way without its source. Some statements credited to popes, cardinals, and reformers are hard to trace, and others have been trimmed until they say more than the author meant. We left out any statement we could not read in its original setting. That habit protects truth, and it also protects the people we quote, who deserve to be represented as they actually wrote.

**Before you share a quote about the Sabbath**
- Find the original document, not a list of quotes
- Read the sentences around it
- Ask who is speaking: the author or an opponent he is reporting
- Check the date and the place
- When you cannot verify it, leave it out

- Read Scripture first : Genesis 2, Exodus 20, Luke 23
- Read the witnesses : Justin, Socrates, Sozomen
- Read the rulings : Constantine and Laodicea
- Compare the statements : Catholic and Protestant in their own words
- Talk it over : With family or a friend

Related: [Resting in His Presence: What the Sabbath Teaches Us About Trust](https://shekinahsda.org/blog/resting-in-his-presence-what-the-sabbath-teaches-us-about-trust/)

## Questions people ask

### Did Constantine change the Sabbath to Sunday?

No, Constantine did not change the Sabbath to Sunday on his own, because Christians were already meeting on Sunday long before his law of AD 321. Justin Martyr describes such a gathering around the middle of the second century. What Constantine did was order civil rest on the day of the Sun in the cities, which gave Sunday standing in Roman law. His law strengthened the custom, but it says nothing about the Sabbath or the fourth commandment.

### Is Saturday the Sabbath?

Yes, Saturday is the seventh day of the week, the day the Bible calls the Sabbath. Luke's account places the Sabbath between the day Jesus died and the first day of the week, and Justin Martyr says that Jesus was "crucified on the day before that of Saturn" and rose the day after it. That places the Sabbath on Saturn's day, the day we call Saturday. Many who worship on Sunday agree on this point, even though they explain the change of worship differently.

### Did the Catholic Church change the Sabbath?

The answer depends on what is meant, because Sunday worship began before there was any decision by a pope or a universal council. Aquinas does credit the institution of the Church and Christian custom for the Lord's Day taking the Sabbath's place, and the Catechism teaches that Sunday's observance replaces that of the Sabbath. Catholics today would add that the practice goes back to the earliest Christians and honors the resurrection. Historically, the fairest summary is that the change grew over centuries through Christian custom, church rulings, and civil law, rather than one act.

### Is Saturday vs Sunday worship a question of salvation?

No, keeping a day does not save anyone, because salvation comes by grace through faith in Jesus Christ. The question is about a faithful response to what God has said, not about earning His love, because obedience to His commandments is the fruit of salvation and never its cause. Justin Martyr's own century shows Christians struggling with this, and his willingness to call Sabbath keeping believers "kinsmen and brethren" is a good reminder to treat one another gently. Millions of Sunday keeping Christians love Jesus sincerely, and God knows every one of them.

## Reflection questions

Take a few quiet minutes with these questions, alone or with your family. When you learned where your own weekly worship habits came from, did the history surprise you, and why? How do you decide between a long custom and the plain words of Scripture when the two seem to point in different directions? And how could you talk about this subject with a Christian friend in a way that leaves them feeling more loved, not less?

## A word of encouragement

History can feel like a heavy subject, but it does not have to weigh you down. If you have kept Sunday all your life, there is no shame in learning something new, and no one is asking you to doubt the faith you have known in Jesus. God has been patient with His people through every century of this story, and He is patient with you. The same Savior who is Lord of the Sabbath still says, "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28, KJV). You can bring your questions to Him without fear.

## A prayer

Father in heaven, thank You for the gift of Your Word and for all who have loved You through the long centuries. Give us honest minds as we read history and humble hearts as we read Scripture. Help us to treat our brothers and sisters with kindness, even when we see things differently. Lead us by Your Spirit into all that You would have us know, and keep our eyes on Jesus, who died and rose for us. In His name we pray, Amen.

# What Happens One Second After Death? Sleep, Soul, and Resurrection

URL: https://shekinahsda.org/blog/what-happens-one-second-after-death/
Category: Bible Answers
Author: Naomi Ellis
Published: 2026-11-02

The Bible describes death as an unconscious sleep, so for the believer the very next moment after the last breath is the voice of Jesus at the resurrection.


You are sitting beside a hospital bed, or lying awake on the night after a funeral, and one small question will not leave you alone. A breath goes out and does not come back. What happens one second after death? Where is the person whose hand you were holding, and what do they know right now?

Everyone around you seems to have an answer. A cousin says your father is looking down on you, a neighbor says he has gone to his reward, and a video describes a tunnel of light. You may have nodded politely while feeling that you still did not know. If that is where you are today, please take your time here.

This article stays with one thing only, the very first moment after the last breath. We will look at what a soul is, what the dead know, why Jesus used the word sleep, and how to read the five texts that seem to say the opposite. Where we are drawing a conclusion rather than repeating a plain statement of Scripture, we will tell you so.

## The short answer

According to the Bible, one second after death a person knows nothing at all, because the dead are unconscious until the resurrection. Jesus called that state sleep. For the one who dies trusting Him, the next conscious moment is His voice calling them out of the grave, however long the sleep has lasted on earth.

That answer rests on two teachings that belong together. The soul is the whole living person, and immortality belongs to God alone, who gives it to His people at the return of Christ. Many sincere Christians read these things differently, so we will set out their reasons fairly as we go.

- Asleep : Paul's word for the believing dead (1 Thessalonians 4:13)
- One voice : All in the graves shall hear it (John 5:28)
- God only : Has immortality by nature (1 Timothy 6:16)

## What happens to the soul after death?

The Bible's answer begins with what a soul is, and in Genesis a soul is what a person is rather than something a person has. When the soul dies, the person has died, and no second self walks on without them. Scripture's first description of a human being is simple.

> "And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul." Genesis 2:7, KJV

Read the last words slowly. Genesis does not say that God placed a soul inside Adam, but that Adam became one when the breath of life met the dust. The Hebrew and Greek words translated "soul" very often mean the whole person, as the Biblical Research Institute scholar Ekkehardt Mueller shows in his study of immortality. So Ezekiel can say, "the soul that sinneth, it shall die" (Ezekiel 18:4, KJV), which would be an odd thing to say of something that cannot die.

When life ends, the same picture runs in reverse. God told Adam, "dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return" (Genesis 3:19, KJV), and the Preacher adds, "Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it" (Ecclesiastes 12:7, KJV). We understand that spirit to be the breath of life God first gave, since Psalm 146:4 speaks of the same moment with the words "His breath goeth forth." The verse is said of everyone who dies, and it says nothing of a conscious person traveling to God.

### Does the Bible teach soul sleep?

The Bible teaches that the dead sleep, though the phrase "soul sleep" itself never appears in Scripture and can mislead. It suggests a separate soul lying dormant somewhere, waiting to be switched back on. What this article teaches is simpler and more serious, namely that the whole person is dead and that only God can give that person life again.

## What do the dead know?

The dead know nothing, according to the plainest verse on the subject: "For the living know that they shall die: but the dead know not any thing" (Ecclesiastes 9:5, KJV). The same chapter says that "there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest" (Ecclesiastes 9:10, KJV). Psalm 146:4 agrees that when the breath goes, "in that very day his thoughts perish." The phrase "in that very day" is about as close as Scripture comes to speaking of the first second.

Some readers answer that Ecclesiastes describes life "under the sun" as it looks from a merely human point of view, and so it should not settle a doctrine. That is a fair objection. Yet the same picture comes from outside Ecclesiastes, from a psalm of praise and from the book of Job. Job says, "So man lieth down, and riseth not" and then asks, "If a man die, shall he live again?" before adding that he will wait "till my change come" (Job 14:12 to 14, KJV).

There is also a tender side to these hard verses. If the dead know nothing, then the mother you buried is not watching you struggle with the bills, and the child you lost is not crying for you. No one you love is frightened, lonely, or waiting in the dark, because waiting requires awareness.

## Is death like sleep in the Bible?

Yes, death is like sleep in the Bible, and Jesus Himself chose that comparison. When His friend died He told the disciples, "Our friend Lazarus sleepeth; but I go, that I may awake him out of sleep" (John 11:11, KJV). They thought He meant ordinary rest, so "Then said Jesus unto them plainly, Lazarus is dead" (John 11:14, KJV). The two sentences explain each other, for the sleep was death, and the waking would be resurrection.

Sleep is a picture rather than a full definition, and we should not press it too far. Wilson Paroschi, writing for the Biblical Research Institute, points out that death is not literally sleep, and that the comparison is there to point us toward the resurrection. Death remains an enemy, and "The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death" (1 Corinthians 15:26, KJV). What the word sleep gives us is a promise that the one who has lain down can be awakened, and that Someone intends to do it.

Listen to the way Martha talked when she met Jesus, four days after her brother was laid in the grave. She did not say that Lazarus was already in glory. She said, "I know that he shall rise again in the resurrection at the last day" (John 11:24, KJV). Jesus pointed her to Himself as "the resurrection, and the life" (John 11:25, KJV). Then He stood before the tomb and "cried with a loud voice, Lazarus, come forth" (John 11:43, KJV), a first glimpse of what that voice will one day do for all His people.

## Is the soul immortal?

No, the Bible never calls the human soul immortal, and it says that God "only hath immortality" (1 Timothy 6:16, KJV). Paul speaks of those who "seek for glory and honour and immortality" (Romans 2:7, KJV), and no one needs to seek what they already own. He also tells us when it arrives: "this mortal must put on immortality" (1 Corinthians 15:53, KJV) at the last trump. Bible students often call this conditional immortality, meaning that life without end is God's gift through Jesus and not a natural property of human beings.

Where then did the idea of an undying soul come from? Mueller traces it to Greek philosophy, noting that Plato called the body the prison of the soul and saw death as the soul's release. His study argues that this thinking had entered Christian teaching by about the third century and shaped it from then on. Others would say the church reached its view by reading Scripture, but the contrast is worth noticing, because for Plato death is a liberation, while for Paul it is an enemy that Christ must defeat.

This is why the resurrection matters so much in the New Testament. Paul writes, "And if Christ be not raised, your faith is vain" and then, "Then they also which are fallen asleep in Christ are perished" (1 Corinthians 15:17 to 18, KJV). He rests everything for the dead on one event, and that event is resurrection.

## Why is the next moment the voice of Jesus?

The next moment is the voice of Jesus because the Bible places the waking of the dead at His word and shows no conscious moments in between. Jesus said, "the hour is coming, in the which all that are in the graves shall hear his voice," and they "shall come forth" (John 5:28 to 29, KJV). Paul wrote to believers who were burying their own, and he described how that hour will come for those who belong to Christ.

> "For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first: Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air: and so shall we ever be with the Lord." 1 Thessalonians 4:16 to 17, KJV

Now put that beside what we have already read, and notice that this step is a conclusion rather than a quotation. No verse says "no time passes for the dead," but if the dead know nothing, then they cannot feel the years go by. Think of a dreamless night, when you close your eyes and open them and cannot say how long you were gone. A woman who died this morning and a shepherd who died in the days of David will both open their eyes to the same voice.

On your side of the grave, that one second is followed by days of grief and years of missing someone. On their side, if we have read Scripture rightly, there is no gap to endure, for the last breath and the shout of the Lord lie side by side. Daniel was promised this kind of rest when he was told, "thou shalt rest, and stand in thy lot at the end of the days" (Daniel 12:13, KJV).

- The last breath: Falling asleep in death: Thoughts cease, and the body returns to the dust (Psalm 146:4).

- Days, years, or centuries: Earth's calendar moves on: The dead know nothing of it (Ecclesiastes 9:5).

- The return of Christ: The voice: The dead in Christ rise first (1 Thessalonians 4:16).

- In the twinkling of an eye: Immortality is given: The mortal puts on immortality (1 Corinthians 15:52 to 53).

- A thousand years later: The second resurrection: Those who refused God's mercy are raised to meet the final judgment (Revelation 20:5).

We should add one honest word about those who do not belong to Christ. They too sleep unconscious, so no one is in torment today, for John 5:29 speaks of two resurrections and Revelation 20:5 places the second a thousand years after the first. We understand those years as the time when God's people share in reviewing His judgment, since "judgment was given unto them" (Revelation 20:4, KJV; see 1 Corinthians 6:2 to 3). The lost are then raised, and "fire came down from God out of heaven, and devoured them" (Revelation 20:9, KJV), which Scripture calls "the second death" (Revelation 20:14, KJV), a final end and not endless torment. We are not able to say who stands where, and we leave that with a God who is perfectly fair.

Related: [What Happens When You Die? What the Bible Really Teaches](https://shekinahsda.org/blog/what-happens-when-you-die-bible/)

## How do other Christians understand the first second?

Many Protestant traditions teach that at death the soul of a believer goes straight to Christ, conscious and at peace, and waits there for the resurrection of the body. Roman Catholic teaching adds purgatory, a final purification for some before they enter heaven, which Protestant theologians reject. John Calvin wrote an entire work against the idea that the dead sleep. These are serious believers who love Jesus.

We share a great deal with them, for all of us confess that Jesus rose bodily, that He is coming again, and that the dead will be raised. Where we differ is on what lies between death and that day. Please read the table below as a guide to a family conversation and not as a scorecard.

| Question | Immediate heaven or hell view | View taught in this article |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What is a soul? | A conscious part that survives the body | The whole living person (Genesis 2:7) |
| Is anyone aware after death? | Yes, with Christ or apart from Him | No, the dead know nothing (Ecclesiastes 9:5) |
| Who is immortal now? | The soul lives on by its nature or by God's sustaining | God only (1 Timothy 6:16) |
| When is the crown given? | Blessing begins at death and is completed later | At His appearing (2 Timothy 4:8) |

## How should we read the five hard texts?

Each of these texts deserves more than a quick reply, and writers at Desiring God and Insight for Living rely on them in good faith. We read each one in its setting and then alongside the plain verses we have already seen. In each case we are offering an interpretation, and we would rather you test it than simply accept it.

### Did Jesus promise the thief paradise that very day?

Jesus certainly promised the thief paradise, but the Bible's wider story suggests that the word "today" belongs to the solemn promise itself rather than to the hour of the thief's arrival. The King James Version reads, "Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise" (Luke 23:43, KJV), and most translations place the comma the same way. Wilson Paroschi notes in Ministry magazine that the comma was most likely absent from Luke's original, and that an idiom like "I command thee this day" (Deuteronomy 6:6, KJV) uses the word to add solemnity. Those who disagree, such as Insight for Living, answer that Scripture records no other time when Jesus said "I say to you today," and that objection deserves to be heard.

Two details persuade us all the same. The thief had asked, "Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom" (Luke 23:42, KJV), which looks ahead to a coming and not to that afternoon. And on the morning of the resurrection Jesus told Mary, "I am not yet ascended to my Father" (John 20:17, KJV). Jesus gave a dying man a certain promise, and it will be kept when the kingdom comes.

### Did Paul expect to be with Christ right after he died?

Paul longed to be with Christ, and from his own point of view that meeting would come as the very next thing he knew. This is the strongest text for the other side, and we want to admit it. He says, "For I am in a strait betwixt two, having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better" (Philippians 1:23, KJV). Desiring God argues that it would be hard to call complete unconsciousness far better, and that is a reasonable thing to feel.

Yet Paul does not say when he expects to be with Christ, and his writing elsewhere answers that question. Two chapters later he says, "we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ" who "shall change our vile body" (Philippians 3:20 to 21, KJV). Facing execution, he writes that "the time of my departure is at hand" and then places his crown "at that day" among those who "love his appearing" (2 Timothy 4:6 to 8, KJV). A man who knows no interval can speak of departing and being with Christ in one breath, and for him that really is far better than the fight he was in.

### What does "absent from the body" mean in 2 Corinthians 5:8?

In 2 Corinthians 5:8 Paul is longing for the resurrection body, not for life without a body. The verse says he is "willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord" but popular quotation often shortens that to say that absence equals presence, which goes further than his words do. The verses before it tell us what he wants: "not for that we would be unclothed, but clothed upon, that mortality might be swallowed up of life" (2 Corinthians 5:4, KJV). Being unclothed is exactly what Paul shrinks from, and his phrase "swallowed up" recalls 1 Corinthians 15:54, where death is "swallowed up in victory" at the resurrection. Other readers see here a time without a body before the resurrection, and we grant that Paul lays out no timeline in this passage.

### Is the rich man and Lazarus a picture of the afterlife?

We understand the rich man and Lazarus to be a parable about how we respond to God's Word, not a description of the first second after death. The details are hard to take literally, for the man who "was buried" still has eyes and a tongue, and he asks for "the tip of his finger in water" (Luke 16:22 to 24, KJV). Kim Papaioannou shows in Ministry magazine that the story has strong similarities with folktales of the ancient world about reversed fortunes and messages from the dead. He also notes that this story gives a person a name, which no other parable of Jesus does, and that some Christians read it as a true account partly for that reason.

Whichever way one takes those details, the weight of the story falls at its end. The rich man begs for someone to warn his brothers, and Abraham refuses: "If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead" (Luke 16:31, KJV). The point is that this life and God's Word are enough.

### Are the souls under the altar conscious in heaven?

We understand the souls under the altar in Revelation 6:9 to 10 as a symbolic scene, and not as a report of what the dead are doing now. John writes, "I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain" and they cry, "How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood" (Revelation 6:9 to 10, KJV). Desiring God sees here a clear sign of conscious saints, and on a first reading that is understandable. But Revelation is a book of symbols, in which a lamb opens seals and horses ride out.

Scripture has already taught us that blood can cry out, for God told Cain, "the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground" (Genesis 4:10, KJV). In the same way, the blood of the martyrs calls to God for justice, and they are told to "rest yet for a little season" (Revelation 6:11, KJV). Even in this vision, the word for them is rest.

**What is plain and what is our reading**
- Plain: the dead know not any thing (Ecclesiastes 9:5)
- Plain: Jesus called death sleep (John 11:11)
- Plain: God only hath immortality (1 Timothy 6:16)
- Plain: the dead in Christ rise at His coming (1 Thessalonians 4:16)
- Our conclusion: the dead do not feel time pass
- Our reading: Luke 16 is a parable and Revelation 6 is symbolic

## What does this change for someone who is grieving?

It changes how you carry the days ahead, even though it does not take the grief away. Paul never told the Thessalonians to stop crying, for he said only that they should "sorrow not, even as others which have no hope" (1 Thessalonians 4:13, KJV). Jesus Himself walked toward a tomb knowing what He was about to do, and still "Jesus wept" (John 11:35, KJV). So your tears are not a failure of faith.

What it can change is the shape of your fear. You do not have to wonder whether the person you love is in pain, or whether they now know about the ways you feel you failed them. Then you can do what Paul told his grieving friends to do: "Wherefore comfort one another with these words" (1 Thessalonians 4:18, KJV).

- Let the tears come : Jesus wept on the way to a grave too
- Lay down the fear : The dead are at rest, not in pain
- Read the promise aloud : 1 Thessalonians 4:13 to 18
- Speak of the morning : Share this hope with a friend
- Trust Jesus today : He is the resurrection and the life

## Questions people ask

### Can a person who has died see or hear me?

No, the Bible says the dead have no part in anything on earth, for they have no more "a portion for ever in any thing that is done under the sun" (Ecclesiastes 9:6, KJV). That can hurt to read, especially if talking to someone at the grave has brought you comfort. Speaking your love aloud is a natural part of grieving, and no one should shame you for it. But you can bring those words to God, who hears every one of them and who holds that person's future in His hands.

### Does the sleep of death mean God has forgotten the dead?

No, the sleep of death does not mean God has forgotten anyone, because a sleeper is someone you intend to wake. Job asked God to "appoint me a set time, and remember me" (Job 14:13, KJV), and he trusted that God would. The faith heroes of Hebrews 11 "received not the promise" so that "they without us should not be made perfect" (Hebrews 11:39 to 40, KJV). God is gathering all of His children to receive the gift together, and no one will arrive late.

### What about people who say they saw heaven during a near death experience?

We want to be gentle here, because many people who describe these moments are sincere and were deeply moved. We do not claim to know what they went through, and this article makes no medical claim about it. What we can say is that Scripture is the measure of every experience, ours included, and the words about Moses and the prophets in Luke 16:31 remind us that God has not left our hope to depend on reports from those who have come back.

Related: [Does Hell Burn Forever? What the Bible Really Says About Hell](https://shekinahsda.org/blog/does-hell-burn-forever-what-the-bible-says/)

## Reflection questions

Take a few quiet minutes with these, by yourself or with someone you trust. Which part of this study brought you comfort, and which part was hard to hear? If you picture your loved one resting and not watching, how might that change what you carry into tomorrow? What would it mean for you today to know that the next voice a believer hears is the voice of Jesus?

## A word of encouragement

If you have read this far with a heavy heart, we are glad you are here. Grief does not move in a straight line, and you may need to come back to these verses more than once. The promise is simply that the One who cried "Lazarus, come forth" has not lost His voice.

One day that voice will sound over every cemetery on earth. The Bible looks beyond even that to the day when "God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying" (Revelation 21:4, KJV). Until then those you have laid to rest are beyond all pain, and you are not alone in the waiting.

## A prayer

Lord Jesus, You wept on the way to the grave of Your friend, so You know what this feels like. We bring You the name we are holding today, and we place it in Your hands. Quiet our fears about the moment of death, and teach us to trust the God who alone has immortality and who gives it freely. Help us to live and to grieve as people who are listening for Your voice. Amen.

# Why Is the Book of Enoch Missing from the Bible? Dead Sea Scrolls & Canon History

URL: https://shekinahsda.org/blog/why-is-the-book-of-enoch-not-in-the-bible/
Category: Bible Answers
Author: Lydia Foster
Published: 2026-11-02

The book of Enoch is a real ancient writing found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, but it was never part of the Hebrew Scriptures or accepted by most of the church, and Jude's use of one saying does not change that.


You are reading the little letter of Jude one evening when a strange line stops you. Jude says that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied about the Lord coming in judgment, yet you cannot remember any such words in Genesis. A quick search brings up videos about a banned book, hidden angels, and a secret the church did not want you to see. Now you are asking a very fair question: why is the book of Enoch not in the Bible?

You do not need to be afraid of that question, and you do not need to wave it away either. The Book of Enoch is a real ancient writing, pieces of it really were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and the letter of Jude really does echo its opening chapter. Those facts are interesting, and they deserve an honest look. They just do not lead where the videos say they lead.

This guide walks through the evidence step by step. We will look at what the book is, what was found at Qumran, what Jude was doing, how Jewish and Christian readers judged it, and why one ancient church reads it differently. At the end we will come back to the deeper question underneath all of this, which is how anyone can know what God has said.

## The short answer

The book of Enoch is not in the Bible because it was never accepted into the Hebrew Scriptures of the Jewish people, and most of the early church came to treat it as a work wrongly credited to Enoch. It was written by later authors, in stages, long after the Flood. Jude's use of one saying does not make the whole book inspired.

That does not mean the book is worthless as history, and it does not mean anyone hid it. Fragments from Qumran show that some Jewish readers valued it before the time of Christ, and early Christian writers such as Tertullian spoke well of it. Other writers doubted it, and over time its standing faded. The one great exception is the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, which still counts Enoch among its books, a view we will describe with the respect it deserves.

- 11 : Enoch manuscripts from Qumran Cave 4
- 5 : Main parts of 1 Enoch
- 66 : Books in the Bible

## What is the book of Enoch?

The book of Enoch, usually called 1 Enoch, is a collection of Jewish writings that claim to record visions given to Enoch, the man in Genesis who walked with God. William Deane, in his older survey of the Pseudepigrapha, says the book "may be said roughly to consist of five parts," with an introduction and a conclusion. Those parts are usually named the Book of the Watchers, the Parables, the Astronomical Book, the Dream Visions, and the Letter of Enoch. The word pseudepigrapha simply means writings published under a borrowed name. Two later works, 2 Enoch and 3 Enoch, also carry his name, but they are separate books.

The Enoch of the Bible is a very different thing from the book that borrowed his name. Scripture tells us a few precious facts about him, and it tells them plainly. He lived before the Flood, he walked closely with the Lord, and he did not see death. Genesis puts it in one quiet sentence.

> "And Enoch walked with God: and he was not; for God took him." Genesis 5:24, KJV

The letter to the Hebrews adds, "By faith Enoch was translated that he should not see death; and was not found, because God had translated him: for before his translation he had this testimony, that he pleased God" (Hebrews 11:5, KJV). Notice what these passages do not say. Neither of them mentions a book, and nowhere does Scripture say that Enoch wrote one. The Bible honors the man, and it does so without pointing us to any writing that carries his name.

### What does 1 Enoch actually teach?

The best known section tells how two hundred angels came down on Mount Hermon, took human wives, and fathered giants, who filled the earth with violence. Later chapters take Enoch on tours of heaven and the ends of the earth, explain the movements of the sun and moon, and describe the coming judgment. Some of it speaks with real moral force about sin and justice, but it adds a great deal that Genesis never says.

## What did the Dead Sea Scrolls reveal about Enoch?

The Dead Sea Scrolls showed that parts of 1 Enoch existed in Aramaic before the time of Christ, and that some Jewish readers copied it. Joseph Fitzmyer, writing in the journal Theological Studies, reports that fragments of this Enoch literature came from Qumran Caves 1, 2, 4, and 6. Cave 4 alone yielded seven fragmentary manuscripts of parts of 1 Enoch and four more of the Astronomical Book. The oldest copies of the Book of the Watchers, he notes, are dated to the early second century BC.

These finds answered an old question about the book's original language. The Aramaic fragments published by J. T. Milik in 1976 made it clear that the core of the work began in Aramaic and was very old, but not nearly old enough. A scroll copied two centuries before Christ cannot take us back to a man who lived before the Flood.

### Were the Parables of Enoch found at Qumran?

No, the Parables, chapters 37 to 71 of 1 Enoch, have not turned up among the Qumran fragments. Fitzmyer records that Milik treated this silence as proof of a later Christian work written in Greek, and he also records his own doubts, calling that reasoning an argument from silence. Scholars still debate when the Parables were written. What everyone can see is that the book did not arrive as a single unit from a single hand. It grew over time, and copies at different stages contained different things.

### Does finding Enoch at Qumran make it Scripture?

No, being found in the caves does not make a writing Scripture, because the caves held far more than the Bible. The collection holds copies of biblical books alongside community rules, hymns, and commentaries on books such as Isaiah and Habakkuk. No one would say that a rule book for a religious community belongs in the Old Testament because it was stored in the same cave. The scrolls tell us what one group of Jewish people read and kept. They do not tell us what the people of Israel as a whole received as the Word of God.

Related: [Did Constantine Really Change the Bible?](https://shekinahsda.org/blog/did-constantine-change-the-bible/)

## Does Jude quote the book of Enoch?

Jude very likely draws on 1 Enoch 1:9, since his words run closely alongside that verse, though he does not name a book. Most scholars accept this link, and some early Christians saw it too. Here is what Jude actually wrote.

> "And Enoch also, the seventh from Adam, prophesied of these, saying, Behold, the Lord cometh with ten thousands of his saints, To execute judgment upon all, and to convince all that are ungodly among them of all their ungodly deeds which they have ungodly committed, and of all their hard speeches which ungodly sinners have spoken against him." Jude 1:14 to 15, KJV

Jude wrote because false teachers had slipped in among believers, and he urged his readers to "earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints" (Jude 1:3, KJV). His point in verses 14 and 15 is simple: the Lord will judge such people, and the warning is older than they think. The picture of the Lord coming with ten thousands also has deep roots in Scripture, since Moses said of Sinai that "he came with ten thousands of saints" (Deuteronomy 33:2, KJV). Jude takes up one solemn saying that serves his pastoral purpose and moves on.

### If Jude quoted it, why is it not Scripture?

Quoting a line from a book does not place the whole book in the Bible, and the New Testament itself shows this. Paul quoted Greek poets in Athens with the words "as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring" (Acts 17:28, KJV). He also cited a writer from Crete: "One of themselves, even a prophet of their own, said, The Cretians are alway liars, evil beasts, slow bellies" (Titus 1:12, KJV). No Christian concludes from this that those pagan writers were inspired. An inspired author can pick out one true statement from a source without vouching for everything around it.

Someone may reasonably answer that Jude goes further than Paul, because he says Enoch "prophesied." Christians have handled that point in more than one way. Some believe Jude was affirming that this one saying truly goes back to the patriarch, passed down through tradition and later preserved in the book. Others believe Jude was using the book's familiar language without settling who wrote it. Both of these are interpretation, not direct statements of Scripture, and either way Jude never says that a book of Enoch is Scripture, and he uses the word "prophesied," not the words "it is written."

**What Jude's words do and do not prove**
- They show that Jude knew a saying linked with Enoch
- They affirm that this saying about judgment is true
- They do not call the book of Enoch Scripture
- They do not vouch for its angels, journeys, or calendars
- They do not make Enoch the author of the whole book

### Did Jude help Enoch or did Enoch hurt Jude?

People today often assume that Jude's quotation raised the standing of Enoch, but some in the early church reasoned the other way around. Jerome, writing in the late fourth century, said of Jude's letter that "because in it he quotes from the apocryphal Book of Enoch it is rejected by many." He goes on to say that it nevertheless came to be reckoned among the Holy Scriptures. So the church accepted Jude in spite of the citation, not as a way of accepting Enoch.

## Why did the Hebrew canon leave it out?

The Hebrew Scriptures never included 1 Enoch, and the first century Jewish historian Josephus describes a closed collection. In Against Apion, he says his people had only twenty two books, which were justly believed to be divine. He adds that later history "hath not been esteemed of the like authority" because there had been no exact succession of prophets after the time of Artaxerxes. He does not name all twenty two, and scholars still discuss how his count lines up with the twenty four books of later Jewish tradition. A book written in the last centuries before Christ, whatever its name, stood outside that line.

This matters for Christians because of a sentence from Paul. He said of the Jewish people, "unto them were committed the oracles of God" (Romans 3:2, KJV). Jesus Himself spoke of "all things" that "must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me" (Luke 24:44, KJV). He used the familiar shape of the Hebrew Scriptures, and He treated them as trustworthy. Enoch was known in His day, yet the Gospels never show Him quoting it by name.

## How did the early church treat the book of Enoch?

Early Christians were divided over Enoch at first, and then its standing steadily declined. James VanderKam, a leading scholar of this literature, shows that the Letter of Barnabas treated Enoch's words as authoritative and that Clement of Alexandria respected the book. Tertullian, writing around AD 200, defended it warmly. Yet even he admitted that some did not receive it because it was not in the Jewish canon, and he leaned on Jude to support his case. That admission tells us the question was already open in his day.

Over the next two centuries the doubts grew stronger. VanderKam notes that Origen, the great Alexandrian teacher, moved away from his earlier confidence, and he later wrote in Against Celsus that the books of Enoch were not generally considered divine in the churches. In AD 367 Athanasius of Alexandria sent his churches a list of the books of Scripture in his Thirty Ninth Festal Letter. Enoch is not on it, and he warned that apocryphal writings "are an invention of heretics, who write them when they choose." Deane sums up the outcome in the West: "By the fifth century the book seems to have sunk out of sight."

### What did Augustine say about Enoch?

Augustine honored Enoch the man and rejected the writings credited to him. In The City of God, Book 18, chapter 38, he asks, "What of Enoch, the seventh from Adam?" He grants that the canonical letter of Jude says Enoch prophesied, and then he explains that the canon has not admitted these writings, "not because the authority of these men who pleased God is rejected," but because they are not believed to be theirs. Their claimed age made it needful to regard them with suspicion, he says, "lest false things should be set forth instead of true." We can honor Enoch and Jude fully while declining a book that merely borrows Enoch's name.

- Early second century BC: Oldest Watchers copies: Aramaic copies of the Book of the Watchers are made, according to Fitzmyer

- First century AD: Jude and Josephus: Jude uses a saying linked with Enoch, while Josephus describes twenty two sacred books

- Around AD 200: Tertullian: He defends Enoch but admits that some reject it because it is outside the Jewish canon

- AD 367: Athanasius: His list of Scripture leaves Enoch out

- Fifth century: Augustine: He explains why the canon does not admit it, and the book fades in the West

- 1773 and 1821: Bruce and Laurence: James Bruce brings Ethiopic copies to Europe, and Richard Laurence publishes an English translation

- 1947 and 1976: Qumran: The first scrolls are found, and Milik publishes the Aramaic Enoch fragments

## Why does the Ethiopian Bible include Enoch?

The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church includes Enoch because it received the book into its own ancient canon, and it continues to treat the book as Scripture. The church's own website says it has 46 books of the Old Testament and 35 books of the New Testament, for a total of 81, and Enoch appears in its Old Testament list. The record does not tell us exactly why Ethiopian authorities reached a different judgment from the rabbis and other churches. What we do know is that Christians everywhere owe this church a real debt. Without the faithful copying done by Ethiopian believers, the complete text of 1 Enoch might have been lost to history.

This article reads the question differently, and it should say why without any disrespect. The same church page explains that for this tradition the Word of God is found in tradition as well as in the Bible, and that the two are received "with equal veneration." This article holds to Scripture alone as the rule of faith, and so it asks a narrower question: did the people who received the oracles of God, and the apostles who followed them, hand this book on as Scripture? On the evidence above, the answer for Enoch is no. Sincere believers can disagree on this while treating one another with respect.

| Question | The 66 books | 1 Enoch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Received in the Hebrew Scriptures? | The 39 Old Testament books, yes | No |
| Written by the person named? | Not all name an author, and this article holds that none rests on a false claim to one | No, it was written long after the Flood |
| Agrees with the rest of Scripture? | Yes, it speaks with one voice | It adds to and differs from the Bible story |
| Treated as Scripture today? | By Christians worldwide | Mainly in the Ethiopian Orthodox tradition |

## What is the difference between the Apocrypha and the Bible?

The Apocrypha usually means the extra Jewish books, such as Tobit and Judith, found in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles but not in the 66 book Bible, while Enoch is not part of that group at all. Protestant Bibles have 66 books, Catholic Bibles have 73, and Eastern Orthodox Bibles have about 76, and Enoch is not canonical in any of the three. So anyone who says Enoch was cut out of a Bible that once held it has the history wrong for nearly all of Christianity. The usual word for books like Enoch is pseudepigrapha, as we saw above. Keeping these terms apart clears away much confusion in biblical canon history.

### Does the content of Enoch conflict with Scripture?

Yes, at some important points, and that is a stronger reason for caution than its date alone. In chapter 22, the spirits of the dead are gathered in hollow places where they are aware and waiting, and the spirit of Abel is heard making its case to heaven. The Bible's own teaching points another way: death is an unconscious state, for "the dead know not any thing" (Ecclesiastes 9:5, KJV), and the hope of the dead lies in the resurrection. The story of angels marrying women is hard to square with Jesus' words about those raised from the dead, who "neither marry, nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven" (Matthew 22:30, KJV).

Christians have read Genesis 6 in different ways, and you should know that. Some, including many in the early centuries, believed the sons of God there were angels, and they are sincere readers of the text. Many other Bible students understand the phrase to mean the godly descendants of Seth who married into the line of Cain, and that is the reading this article finds most faithful to the context of Genesis. Jude 6 does speak of angels who left their proper place, and many scholars hear an echo of Enoch there. Yet Jude 6 itself says nothing of marriage, though some readers connect it with the sin of Sodom named in verse 7, and Revelation 12:7 to 9 places the fall of Satan and his angels in a war in heaven.

## Why is Scripture alone the rule of faith?

Scripture alone is the rule of faith because it is the only writing we can be sure was given by God for that purpose. Paul wrote, "All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness" (2 Timothy 3:16, KJV). Peter explained how it came to us: "For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost" (2 Peter 1:21, KJV). Isaiah gives the test that applies to every other voice: "To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them" (Isaiah 8:20, KJV). God's people did not give the Bible its authority, since they could only receive what He had already inspired.

This does not mean that old books are useless. Reading 1 Enoch can help a student understand how some Jews thought in the centuries before Christ, in much the same way that reading Josephus does. The difference lies in what the reader does with it. A history book can inform us, but only the Word of God can bind our conscience. When a video promises secret knowledge, we can set that claim beside the Bible and let the Bible have the final word.

- Compare its teaching : Does it agree with the law and the testimony?
- Ask who received it : Was it handed on as Scripture by God's people?
- Ask who wrote it : Does its claim to an author hold up?
- Keep the proportion : Build your faith on plain Scripture, not on hidden stories

## Questions people ask

### Was the book of Enoch banned by the church?

The evidence points to a slow fading rather than a dramatic ban. Christian writers argued about Enoch for centuries, and copies of it were still known in the East after it had faded in the West. Deane notes that extracts preserved by the Byzantine chronicler Syncellus, who wrote around AD 800, show that it lasted longer in the Eastern Church. Readers weighed it and did not receive it as Scripture, and no hidden group erased it. If anything, the fact that the book survived shows how hard it would have been to hide.

### Is it wrong for a Christian to read the book of Enoch?

It is not wrong to read it as a historical document, as long as you do not treat it as the Word of God. Scholars read it for just that reason, and it can shed light on the world Jude lived in. Still, it is wise to start with the Bible itself, especially if you are new in faith, because stories about angels and giants can easily crowd out the gospel. If you do read Enoch, read it slowly, with your Bible open beside it.

### Could there be more books that God wants in the Bible?

No, the 66 books are the complete Bible, and they are sufficient for salvation. Paul told Timothy that the Scriptures he had known from childhood could make him "wise unto salvation" through faith in Christ, as 2 Timothy 3:15 says. Ancient discoveries have helped us understand the Bible better, but they have not produced a lost book that reshapes the gospel. You can open your 66 book Bible with confidence that nothing you need for eternal life is missing.

## How can you handle claims like this in everyday life?

The most useful habit you can build is checking the claim against the source, the way the believers in Berea did. They "searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so" (Acts 17:11, KJV). When a new claim reaches you, slow down before you share it, and ask what the original texts say and who is making the claim. Then read the passage in its full setting, as we did with Jude. A family that reads a chapter together each evening will also notice quickly when a strange teaching does not sound like the Jesus of the Gospels.

Related: [What Happens When You Die? What the Bible Really Teaches](https://shekinahsda.org/blog/what-happens-when-you-die-bible/)

## Reflection questions

When you hear a claim about a hidden or banned book, what is your first reaction, and what would it look like to test it the way the Bereans did? Which do you find easier to trust, the short and restrained words of Scripture or a longer story that fills in every detail? What is one passage you could read this week to know the voice of the real Bible a little better?

## A word of encouragement

If this subject has unsettled you, take heart. The Bible has been examined by friends and critics for centuries, and the discoveries at Qumran have given us more reason to trust it, not less. You are not missing a secret chapter that holds the key to your life with God. The same Lord who walked with Enoch is willing to walk with you today, and He has already told you what you need to know. "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path" (Psalm 119:105, KJV).

## A prayer

Father in heaven, thank You for speaking to us through Your Word. When strange claims and loud voices make us uneasy, give us a calm mind and an honest heart. Teach us to love the Scriptures and to test everything by them. Help us to walk with You as Enoch did, trusting Jesus until the day we see Him. We ask this in His name, amen.

## Your next step

If you would like to study these questions with someone instead of sorting them out alone, we invite you to begin a free Bible study. Bring your questions about the canon, about Jude, or about how the Bible came to us, and open the Scriptures with people who love them. Shekinah church in Alvarado, Texas, offers these studies free of charge. The goal is simple: that you read the Word for yourself and meet the Jesus it describes.
