# Did Constantine Really Change the Bible? The Truth About the Council of Nicaea (325 AD)

URL: https://shekinahsda.org/blog/did-constantine-change-the-bible/
Category: Bible Answers
Author: Elijah Grant
Published: 2026-10-31

Constantine never edited the Bible and the Council of Nicaea never voted on its books; here is what the ancient sources really show, with a timeline and study guide.


You are scrolling through your phone late at night when a short video stops you. A confident voice says that the Roman emperor Constantine sat down with a group of bishops in the fourth century, picked the books he liked, burned the rest, and voted Jesus into being God. The video has millions of views and thousands of comments. Some people sound angry, some sound afraid, and some simply ask the question you are now asking yourself: did Constantine change the Bible?

It is a fair question, and you deserve a careful answer rather than a slogan. The good news is that we do not have to guess. The men who were at the Council of Nicaea wrote about it, Roman law codes still preserve Constantine's decrees, and more than a hundred New Testament manuscripts, most of them fragments, copied before AD 325 survive in museums and libraries today. When we lay those sources side by side, a clear picture appears.

This article is written as a study guide. You will find a timeline, the ancient documents with links so you can read them yourself, the Bible texts that matter most, and questions to think through with your family or study group. Like the Bereans in Acts, who "searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so" (Acts 17:11, KJV), you are invited to check every claim.

## The short answer

No. Constantine did not change the Bible, and the Council of Nicaea in AD 325 never voted on which books belong in Scripture. The council met to answer one urgent question, whether Jesus Christ is fully God or a created being, and it also discussed the date of Easter and church order. The Gospels and Paul's letters were already being copied and read as Scripture long before Constantine was born.

What the evidence does show is something different and important. Constantine did shape Christian practice through Roman law, most famously with a civil decree in AD 321 that ordered rest on "the venerable day of the Sun." That law made Sunday a legal day of rest across the empire, but it did not change a single word of the Bible. Keeping those two things apart, the text of Scripture and the customs that grew up around it, is the key to understanding this whole story.

- AD 325 : Council of Nicaea meets
- 250+ : Bishops present, according to Eusebius
- 0 : Canons about which books belong in the Bible

## What is the viral claim about Constantine and the Bible?

The popular claim says that Constantine and the bishops at Nicaea handpicked the 66 books of the Bible, threw out the gospels they disliked, and invented the idea that Jesus is God. In its most famous modern form, the story comes from the 2003 novel The Da Vinci Code, where a character claims that Constantine collated a new Bible and that the divinity of Jesus was decided by "a relatively close vote." The novel is fiction, but many people now repeat its lines as if they were history.

Part of the claim is true, and that is what makes it convincing. Constantine really did call the council, he really did attend it, and the bishops really did debate and vote on several questions. The problem is everything that has been added. Neither the records of the council nor the writers who were there say anything about choosing books of Scripture, and the vote on the nature of Christ was not close at all.

### Why do these stories spread so easily?

Stories like this spread because they mix a few real names and dates with a dramatic secret, and because most of us have never been shown the original sources. A short video cannot quote Eusebius, Athanasius, Irenaeus, and the Roman law codes in sixty seconds. When people are never given the evidence, a confident voice can fill the silence. That is why going back to the sources matters so much.

## What really happened at the Council of Nicaea?

The Council of Nicaea met in AD 325 in the city of Nicaea, which is today İznik in Turkey. Constantine called it because the churches of the eastern empire were divided, and he wanted unity. Eusebius of Caesarea, a bishop who attended, wrote that "the number of bishops exceeded two hundred and fifty," along with presbyters and deacons too many to count (Life of Constantine 3.8).

The main problem was a teaching spread by Arius, a priest from Alexandria in Egypt. Arius taught that the Son of God was not eternal but was created by the Father, so that there was a time when the Son did not exist. Many believers were deeply troubled, because Scripture presents Jesus as fully divine. The bishops rejected the teaching of Arius and wrote a creed declaring that the Son is "of one substance" with the Father. Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that the council condemned Arius and affirmed the Son's full equality with the Father.

### What else did the bishops discuss?

Eusebius explains that the second reason for the council was the long dispute over when to celebrate Easter, with churches in different regions keeping it on different days (Life of Constantine 3.5). The bishops also issued about twenty short rules, called canons, on church order. They dealt with how bishops are chosen, clergy moving from church to church, lending money at interest, and how to receive people who had fallen away during persecution. The canons themselves, which Britannica summarizes, show these topics, and not one of them mentions which books belong in the Bible.

### Did Athanasius say the council chose the books of the Bible?

No. Athanasius of Alexandria was at Nicaea as a young assistant to his bishop, and he later spent decades defending what the council taught about Christ. His writings about the council focus on the debate with the followers of Arius over the Son's divine nature. Decades later, in AD 367, Athanasius did write a letter that listed the 27 books of the New Testament, and we will look at it below. That list came from a pastor teaching his churches what they had long received, not from a vote at Nicaea.

**What Nicaea did and did not do**
- It answered whether Jesus is fully God, rejecting the teaching of Arius
- It addressed the date of Easter and church order
- It issued about twenty canons, none about the books of Scripture
- It did not create, edit, or vote on the Bible
- It did not invent belief in the divinity of Christ, which Christians held long before

## Was Jesus called God before the Council of Nicaea?

Yes, many times and in many places. The New Testament itself speaks plainly. John begins his Gospel with these words: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1, KJV). After the resurrection, Thomas falls before the risen Lord and says, "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28, KJV). These words were written in the first century, more than two hundred years before Nicaea.

Writers outside the Bible confirm the same faith. Around AD 110, Ignatius, a church leader in Antioch, wrote a letter to the believers in Ephesus that opens by speaking of "Jesus Christ, our God." Around AD 112, a Roman governor named Pliny the Younger, who was not a Christian at all, reported to the emperor that Christians met "on a fixed day before dawn" and sang "a hymn to Christ as to a god" (Letters 10.96). A pagan official noticed that Christians worshiped Jesus as divine two centuries before Constantine.

So the council did not invent the belief that Jesus is God. It defended an old belief against a newer teaching that denied it. The vote was not close either. Of the bishops present, only two refused to sign, and the council condemned the teaching of Arius.

## When were the books of the Bible recognized?

Long before Constantine. The Old Testament Scriptures were already received by the Jewish people and quoted by Jesus Himself. After His resurrection, Jesus "beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself" (Luke 24:27, KJV). The early church inherited these Scriptures and read them as the Word of God.

The New Testament writings were read as Scripture within the lifetime of the apostles. Paul told the believers in Colossae, "when this epistle is read among you, cause that it be read also in the church of the Laodiceans" (Colossians 4:16, KJV). His letters were shared from church to church. Peter, writing about Paul's letters, says that some people twist them "as they do also the other scriptures" (2 Peter 3:16, KJV). In other words, Peter already placed Paul's letters alongside the other Scriptures.

### What do the early church writers show?

Around AD 180, Irenaeus of Lyon wrote that "it is not possible that the Gospels can be either more or fewer in number than they are," meaning Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John (Against Heresies 3.11.8). That was nearly a century and a half before Nicaea. The four Gospels were already the settled Gospels of the church across the empire.

The first list that names exactly the 27 books of our New Testament comes from Athanasius in his Easter letter of AD 367, more than forty years after Nicaea. He lists the four Gospels, Acts, the seven general letters, the fourteen letters of Paul, and Revelation, and then he writes, "These are fountains of salvation, that they who thirst may be satisfied with the living words they contain." Athanasius was not inventing a list. He was naming the books the churches had long recognized, so that his people would not be confused by other writings.

### What do the oldest manuscripts show?

The handwritten copies themselves tell the same story. One of the most important is a papyrus book known as P46, which contains the letters of Paul and is dated to about AD 180 to 200. Part of it is kept at the Chester Beatty Library in Dublin and part at the University of Michigan. Christians were copying Paul's letters together, as a collection of Scripture, more than a century before Constantine called the council.

- About AD 110: Ignatius calls Jesus "our God": A church leader in Antioch writes to Ephesus.

- About AD 112: Pliny reports Christian worship: Christians sing "a hymn to Christ as to a god."

- About AD 180: Irenaeus names four Gospels: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John are already settled.

- About AD 180 to 200: P46 is copied: Paul's letters circulate together as Scripture.

- AD 321: Constantine's civil decree: Rest is ordered on "the venerable day of the Sun."

- AD 325: Council of Nicaea: Bishops answer Arius on the divinity of Christ.

- AD 367: Athanasius lists 27 books: The New Testament the churches had received.

## What did Constantine actually change?

Constantine did influence Christian life, and honesty requires us to say so. The clearest example is a law he issued on March 7, 321. The church historian Philip Schaff gives it this way: "On the venerable Day of the Sun let the magistrates and people residing in cities rest, and let all workshops be closed." The law allowed farmers in the countryside to keep working. It is preserved in the later Roman law collection known as the Code of Justinian.

Notice what this law is and what it is not. It is a civil decree from the emperor about work and rest in Roman cities. It uses the old pagan name for the day, the day of the Sun, and Schaff points out that it makes no reference to the Ten Commandments or to the resurrection of Christ. It did not touch the text of the Bible. The fourth commandment still read exactly as it always had: "the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God" (Exodus 20:10, KJV).

### Why does the difference matter?

It matters because the real question is not whether someone edited the Bible, but whether we follow the Bible or the customs that grew up beside it. Jesus warned, and the warning is for every one of us, about worship that teaches "for doctrines the commandments of men" (Mark 7:7, KJV). The Scriptures have been carefully preserved. Customs, laws, and traditions have sometimes moved away from them over the centuries. When we see that difference clearly, we can stop worrying that the Bible was secretly rewritten, and start asking the more personal question of whether our own faith and practice match what Scripture plainly says.

| Claim | What the evidence shows |
| --- | --- |
| Constantine chose the books of the Bible | No council canon, and no writer at Nicaea, mentions choosing books |
| Nicaea invented the divinity of Jesus | John 1:1, Ignatius, and Pliny show Jesus was worshiped as God long before |
| The vote on Jesus was close | Only two bishops refused to sign |
| Nothing changed under Constantine | His AD 321 civil decree made Sunday the empire's legal day of rest |

Related: [Why worship on the seventh day? Read the Bible story of the Sabbath](https://shekinahsda.org/blog/why-do-seventh-day-adventists-worship-on-saturday/)

## How can you study this history for yourself?

Start with the Bible itself, then read the ancient witnesses in their own words. Read John 1, Colossians 4, and 2 Peter 3 to see how the first Christians spoke about Jesus and about Scripture. Then open the sources listed at the end of this article: Eusebius on the council, Irenaeus on the four Gospels, Pliny's letter to the emperor, the letter of Ignatius, and the Easter letter of Athanasius. Each one is short enough to read in one sitting.

As you read, ask three simple questions of every claim you hear online. Who said it first? What source do they quote? When was that source written? A claim about AD 325 that cannot point to a document from that time deserves caution. Paul's counsel is still the best rule for anyone studying history or faith: "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good" (1 Thessalonians 5:21, KJV).

- Read Scripture first : John 1, Colossians 4, 2 Peter 3
- Read the witnesses : Eusebius, Irenaeus, Pliny, Athanasius
- Check the dates : Who wrote it, and when?
- Compare with the Bible : Does the claim match what Scripture says?
- Talk it over : Study with family or a friend

## Questions people ask

### Did the Council of Nicaea decide which books are in the Bible?

No, the Council of Nicaea did not decide which books are in the Bible. Its creed answered the teaching of Arius, the bishops discussed the date of Easter, and its twenty canons dealt with church order, and none of them lists or votes on books of Scripture. The four Gospels were already settled by Irenaeus around AD 180, and the first exact list of all 27 New Testament books comes from Athanasius in AD 367, more than forty years after the council.

### Did Constantine burn other gospels?

There is no record from the council or from the writers who were there that Constantine burned other gospels at Nicaea. Writings such as the so called gnostic gospels were already rejected by church leaders like Irenaeus in the second century, long before Constantine, because they taught ideas that contradicted the apostles. The story of a dramatic burning at Nicaea comes from modern retellings, not from ancient sources.

### Was Constantine a Christian?

Constantine favored Christianity, helped end the persecution of believers, and called the Council of Nicaea, but he was not baptized until shortly before his death in AD 337. Britannica describes him at the time of the council as an unbaptized catechumen, someone still preparing for baptism. His laws mixed Christian and Roman customs, which is why it is wise to measure his decisions by Scripture rather than assume they all came from the Bible.

### Can we trust that the Bible we read today is accurate?

Yes, we have strong reasons to trust that the Bible we read today faithfully preserves what was first written. Thousands of handwritten copies survive, some like P46 from around AD 200, and scholars compare them carefully. The Bible itself promises, "The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever" (Isaiah 40:8, KJV). History and manuscripts agree that God has kept His Word.

## Reflection questions

Take a few minutes with these questions, alone or with your family or study group. When you hear a dramatic claim about the Bible online, what is your first reaction, and how could you begin checking it against the sources? Why do you think it matters that Christians worshiped Jesus as God long before any emperor got involved? And where in your own life might a custom or tradition have quietly taken the place of something Scripture plainly teaches?

## A word of encouragement

If stories like the one about Constantine have ever shaken your faith, you are not alone, and you have nothing to fear from honest questions. The evidence points in a hopeful direction. The Word of God was received, copied, and treasured by ordinary believers long before councils and emperors, and it has come down to us with remarkable care. Paul wrote that "all scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness" (2 Timothy 3:16, KJV). You can open your Bible today with confidence that the same Lord who spoke through it then is speaking to you now.

## A prayer

Heavenly Father, thank You for preserving Your Word through every century, through persecution and confusion, so that we can read it today. When we hear voices that make us doubt, give us wisdom to search the Scriptures and courage to follow where they lead. Thank You for Jesus, the Word who was with God and who is God, and help us love Him and obey Him with all our hearts. In His name we pray, Amen.

## Your next step

If this study helped you, the best next step is to keep going with the Bible itself. Shekinah church in Alvarado, Texas offers free personal Bible studies in Kreyòl, French, or English, at church, by phone, or online, and you can study at your own pace through our free Bible Study Library. You are also warmly welcome to join us any Saturday for Sabbath School at 10:00 AM and the Divine Service at 11:00 AM at 205 E Carver St, where you can ask your questions in person with people who love to open the Bible together.

# Giving Thanks When Life Is Hard: Bible Verses About Gratitude

URL: https://shekinahsda.org/blog/giving-thanks-when-life-is-hard/
Category: Devotional
Author: Rachel Simmons
Published: 2026-10-26

Some of the strongest words of thanks in Scripture were spoken in prison, hunger, and loss, and they can teach us to give thanks in every season, not only the easy ones.


The table is set, the house smells like something good, and everyone is supposed to be grateful. Yet one chair sits empty this year, the bills on the counter have not gone away, and the doctor still has not called back. Somewhere between the blessing and the first bite, you wonder how anyone can say thank you when life feels this heavy. If that is where you are as November begins, this devotional is for you.

Most lists of Bible verses about gratitude are beautiful, but they can feel like they were written for people whose lives are going well. The surprising thing is that many of the strongest words of thanks in Scripture were spoken by people in prison, in hunger, in sickness, and in national disaster. Their thanksgiving was not a denial of pain. It was a decision to keep looking at God while the pain was still present.

In the pages below we will walk slowly through a handful of those passages and the stories behind them. Then we will turn them into simple habits for your mornings, your family table, and your Sabbath. You do not have to feel thankful to begin. You only have to be willing to take the next small step.

## The short answer

The Bible does not ask us to be thankful for every painful thing that happens. It asks us to give thanks in every situation, because God is still good, still present, and still working in it. Paul wrote, "In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you" (1 Thessalonians 5:18). Notice the small word "in." Gratitude in hard times is not pretending the hard thing is good; it is remembering that God has not left us inside it.

> "In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you." 1 Thessalonians 5:18, KJV

That verse sits beside two other short commands in the same passage, to rejoice and to pray continually (1 Thessalonians 5:16 to 17). Together they describe a heart that keeps turning toward God all day long. Thankfulness, in other words, is less like a feeling that visits us once a year and more like a direction we choose again and again.

**What biblical gratitude is not**
- It is not pretending you are fine
- It is not thanking God for evil or abuse
- It is not a test you fail when you cry
- It is trusting that God is good while you wait

## Thankful in prison: Paul and the Philippians

Paul wrote the letter to the Philippians while he was a prisoner. He tells his readers that "my bonds in Christ are manifest in all the palace, and in all other places" (Philippians 1:13). He did not know how his case would end. Yet this short letter is full of joy, and it contains one of the best loved invitations to grateful prayer in the whole Bible.

> "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus." Philippians 4:6 to 7, KJV

"Be careful for nothing" means do not be anxious about anything. Paul does not tell the Philippians to stop asking God for help. He tells them to bring every request, and to wrap those requests in thanksgiving. The promise that follows is not that every problem will vanish, but that God's peace will stand guard over the heart and mind.

A few verses later Paul adds, "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content" (Philippians 4:11). The word "learned" is a gift to anyone who finds gratitude hard. Paul was not born content. He grew into it through seasons of plenty and seasons of hunger (Philippians 4:12), and so can we.

## When the fields are empty: Habakkuk's song

The prophet Habakkuk lived in a frightening time. His book opens with honest complaints to God about violence and injustice, and God answers that the Chaldeans, the armies of Babylon, are coming (Habakkuk 1:6). Habakkuk does not hide his fear. By the end of the book, though, he sings one of the most courageous songs of thanks in Scripture.

> "Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls: Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation." Habakkuk 3:17 to 18, KJV

For a farming people, this list describes total loss: no fruit, no oil, no grain, no animals. Habakkuk is not grateful because the harvest came in. He is grateful because the God of his salvation had not gone anywhere. His very next line says, "The LORD God is my strength" (Habakkuk 3:19).

## Entering His gates: the song of Psalm 100

Psalm 100 carries a simple title in the King James Version: "A Psalm of praise." It is only five verses long, and it invites "all ye lands" to come into God's presence with joy. The psalm pictures worshipers walking through the gates and into the courts of God's house, and it gives them words for that walk. For us, it shows that thanksgiving is the doorway into worship.

> "Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise: be thankful unto him, and bless his name. For the LORD is good; his mercy is everlasting; and his truth endureth to all generations." Psalm 100:4 to 5, KJV

Look at the reason the psalm gives for thanks. It is not "because life is easy" but "for the LORD is good." His mercy is everlasting and His truth lasts through every generation, including yours. Even the book of Lamentations, written in grief over a ruined city, holds on to the same hope: "They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness" (Lamentations 3:23).

## The one who turned back: the ten lepers

As Jesus traveled toward Jerusalem, ten men with leprosy met Him and "stood afar off" (Luke 17:12). They cried out, "Jesus, Master, have mercy on us" (Luke 17:13). Jesus told them to show themselves to the priests, and "as they went, they were cleansed" (Luke 17:14). All ten received the miracle, but the story does not end there.

- 10 : men cleansed on the road
- 1 : turned back to give thanks
- 9 : never came back

> "And one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, and with a loud voice glorified God, And fell down on his face at his feet, giving him thanks: and he was a Samaritan." Luke 17:15 to 16, KJV

The man who returned was a Samaritan, an outsider to many of the people around Jesus. Jesus asked, "Were there not ten cleansed? but where are the nine?" (Luke 17:17). Then He said to the grateful man, "Arise, go thy way: thy faith hath made thee whole" (Luke 17:19). Nine received healing for their skin, but the one who came back received something deeper: a face to face encounter with the Healer Himself.

## What gratitude does in us

Scripture calls us to thanksgiving because God deserves it, but it also shapes the person who gives it. Researchers have noticed something similar. Harvard Health Publishing reported on a 2024 study of more than 49,000 older women in the Nurses' Health Study, which found that women in the top third for gratitude had a 9% lower risk of dying over the next four years than women in the bottom third. The authors are careful to say the study shows an association, not proof, and that the women studied may not represent everyone.

We do not give thanks to live longer, and gratitude is never a cure for grief or illness. Still, it is encouraging to see careful research point in the same direction as the psalmist who said, "It is a good thing to give thanks unto the LORD" (Psalm 92:1). That psalm has a meaningful title too. It is "A Psalm or Song for the sabbath day."

## Gratitude in every season: practical habits

Gratitude grows like Paul's contentment did, through practice. Here is a simple comparison of how hard seasons and good seasons can both become places of thanks. You do not need to do all of these at once. Choose one and start this week.

| Season | What thanks can sound like | A verse to hold |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grief or loss | Lord, thank You that I am not alone in this | Lamentations 3:23 |
| Money worries | Thank You for today's bread, and I trust You with tomorrow | Philippians 4:6 to 7 |
| Sickness | Thank You for every caring hand, and for Your peace tonight | Psalm 100:5 |
| A season of plenty | Help me remember You are the giver of every good thing | Deuteronomy 8:10 |

### At the family table

Moses told Israel, "When thou hast eaten and art full, then thou shalt bless the LORD thy God for the good land which he hath given thee" (Deuteronomy 8:10). The table has always been a place to remember God's goodness. This November, try going around the table once a week and letting each person name one thing they are thankful for, even small children. On hard weeks, give everyone permission to say something honest first and then one thing they still thank God for.

Related: [Five Ways to Build Faith at the Dinner Table](https://shekinahsda.org/blog/five-ways-to-build-faith-at-the-dinner-table/)

### Every Sabbath as a weekly Thanksgiving

Thanksgiving Day comes once a year, but God gave us a day of thanks every week. The Seventh-day Adventist Fundamental Belief 20 describes the Sabbath as "a day of delightful communion with God and one another" and "a celebration of God's creative and redemptive acts." When sunset arrives on Friday, you might light a candle, read Psalm 92 together, and name the ways God carried your family through the week. At Shekinah, our church family also shares a meal after the Sabbath service, and there are few better places to practice gratitude than around a shared table.

- Wake with one thanks : Before checking your phone, thank God for one specific thing
- Pray with thanksgiving : Name a blessing before each request, as Philippians 4:6 teaches
- Turn back : Like the Samaritan, thank God when a prayer is answered
- Say it out loud : Thank a person who has helped you this week
- Close the week well : Use Friday sunset to remember what God has done

### Gratitude across languages and generations

Our worship at Shekinah is in Kreyòl and English, and a heartfelt "mèsi, Senyè" reaches heaven just as surely as "thank You, Lord." Many Haitian families, in Haiti and across the diaspora, carry memories of real loss, including the earthquake that struck on January 12, 2010. Giving thanks in those memories does not mean anyone should be expected to be strong all the time or to hide their tears. It means bringing the whole story, the sorrow and the mercy, to the God who holds both. Gratitude that has walked through hardship is often the kind that speaks most deeply to the next generation.

## When thankfulness feels impossible

Some seasons are so dark that the words will not come. The Bible makes room for that, too, with whole psalms of lament. If you cannot say thank you yet, begin by telling God the truth about how you feel, as Habakkuk did, and ask Him to help you see one sign of His care.

Remember Paul and Silas, beaten and locked in stocks in Philippi. "And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them" (Acts 16:25). Their song did not come before midnight; it came in it. Your thanks, even if it is quiet and trembling, may be the very thing someone else near you needs to hear.

## Questions people ask

### What does the Bible say about giving thanks in hard times?

The Bible says to give thanks in every situation, not for every painful thing, because God is still good, still present, and still working in it. Paul wrote in 1 Thessalonians 5:18 that "In every thing give thanks," and the small word "in" makes all the difference. Gratitude in hard times is not pretending the hard thing is good. It is remembering that God has not left us inside it.

### Do I have to thank God for the bad things that happen?

No, biblical gratitude never asks you to thank God for evil, abuse, or the painful thing itself. Scripture asks us to give thanks in every circumstance, trusting that God is good while we wait. Gratitude is not pretending you are fine, and it is not a test you fail when you cry. The prophet Habakkuk shows the way, because he rejoiced in the God of his salvation while the fields were still empty (Habakkuk 3:17 to 18).

### What Bible verse says to give thanks in everything?

The Bible verse that tells us to give thanks in everything is 1 Thessalonians 5:18, which reads in the King James Version, "In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you." It sits beside two other short commands in 1 Thessalonians 5:16 to 17, to rejoice and to pray continually. Philippians 4:6 also asks us to bring every request to God with thanksgiving. Together these passages describe a heart that keeps turning toward God all day long.

### What should I do when I cannot feel thankful?

When you cannot feel thankful, begin by telling God the truth about how you feel, as the prophet Habakkuk did, and ask Him to help you see one sign of His care. The Bible makes room for that honesty with whole psalms of lament. You do not have to feel thankful to begin, because gratitude grows through practice, just as Paul said he had "learned" contentment in Philippians 4:11. Like Paul and Silas singing at midnight in Acts 16:25, even a quiet and trembling thank you is a real offering to God.

## Reflection questions

Take a few quiet minutes with these questions, alone or with your family. Which of the people in these passages, Paul, Habakkuk, the psalmist, or the Samaritan, feels most like you right now, and why? What is one thing God has done for you this year that you have never stopped to thank Him for? Who in your life needs to hear your thanks before Thanksgiving Day arrives?

## A word of encouragement

You do not have to wait until everything is fixed to be grateful, and you do not have to pretend everything is fixed in order to give thanks. God's mercy is new this morning, and His faithfulness will still be there tonight. The same Jesus who welcomed one thankful man at His feet welcomes you, whatever this season holds. Every small "thank You" is a step toward Him, and He is never too far away to hear it.

## A prayer

Father in heaven, thank You that Your mercy is everlasting and Your truth endures to all generations. In this season, some of us are rejoicing and some of us are hurting, and You see each heart. Teach us, like Paul, to learn contentment, and like the Samaritan, to turn back and thank You. Fill our tables, our homes, and our Sabbaths with gratitude, and let Your peace guard our hearts in Jesus. In His name we pray, Amen.

## Your next step

If this season is heavy for you, you do not have to carry it alone. Our church family would be honored to pray with you and for you, and you can share as much or as little as you like. Share a request through our prayer request page today, and know that a church family in Alvarado is lifting your name to God. You are always welcome to join us for Sabbath worship at 205 E Carver St, too.

# Pikliz: The Spicy Haitian Slaw That Brightens Every Sabbath Plate

URL: https://shekinahsda.org/blog/pikliz-the-spicy-haitian-slaw/
Category: Recipes
Author: Josephine Pierre
Published: 2026-10-26

Make an original, plant based pikliz with a milder option, learn how to keep it safe and crisp in the fridge, and bring it to your Sabbath and Thanksgiving tables.


Picture a Sabbath lunch after a long, joyful morning of worship. The rice and beans are steaming, the plantains are golden, and the whole table smells like home. Then someone opens the refrigerator, sets down a jar of bright orange and white slaw, and the plate suddenly feels complete. That little jar is pikliz, and for many Haitian families a meal simply does not feel finished without it.

Maybe you grew up with pikliz and never learned to make it yourself. Maybe you are new to Haitian food and keep hearing friends talk about that spicy cabbage in the jar. Or maybe Thanksgiving is coming, someone asked you to bring a side dish, and you want something fresh to balance all the rich food. Whatever brought you here, you are in the right kitchen.

In this article we will share an original, fully plant based pikliz recipe with a milder option for children and tender palates. We will also cover the questions people ask most, like how long pikliz lasts, whether it is fermented, and what to eat with it. Because this is a condiment made with very hot peppers and raw vegetables, we will take time on food safety, using guidance from poison control, university extension services, and FoodSafety.gov.

## The short answer

Pikliz is a Haitian condiment of thinly shredded cabbage, carrots, onion, bell pepper, garlic, and hot peppers, covered in vinegar and left to steep in the refrigerator. It is ready to eat in about a day and tastes even better after two or three days. Kept cold in a clean jar with the vegetables under the vinegar, it will last for weeks, though it is a refrigerator food and never a shelf stable canned product. Its heat comes from scotch bonnet peppers, called piman bouk in Kreyòl, and you can control that heat completely.

- 1 day : Until your pikliz is ready to eat
- 40°F : Or colder for your refrigerator
- 3 months : Longest fridge time in extension guidance

## What pikliz is and where it comes from

### A condiment at the heart of the Haitian table

Researchers writing in the Journal of Ethnic Foods describe pikliz as a condiment made from shredded cabbage and carrot with a generous amount of hot pepper and spices, all immersed in vinegar or lemon juice. They note that it has long been prepared at the household level in Haiti and that many Haitian dishes are not considered complete without a portion of pikliz beside them. The same study describes pikliz as a symbol of Haitian identity for families in Haiti and abroad. Today you can even find commercial jars in many American supermarkets, but nothing quite compares to a batch made in your own kitchen.

Many people know pikliz as the partner to fried meats, and it is true that it is often served that way. Yet the heart of pikliz has always been vegetables, vinegar, and pepper. That makes it a natural fit for Adventist kitchens, where many of us enjoy plant based meals. A spoonful of pikliz brings brightness and crunch to beans, rice, plantains, and vegetable patties just as well.

### Is pikliz fermented?

The answer depends on who you ask and how the jar is made. The researchers in the Journal of Ethnic Foods describe some natural fermentation taking place as pikliz sits, with helpful bacteria adding acid and flavor over time. Many home recipes, including ours, get their sourness from vinegar right from the first day, so they work like a quick refrigerator pickle. Either way, the recipe below is meant to be kept cold from the moment you fill the jar.

## The recipe: Shekinah style pikliz

This is our own family style version, written to be simple and forgiving. Use a sharp knife or a mandoline to slice the cabbage as thin as you can, because thin shreds soak up the vinegar and stay pleasantly crisp. If you use a mandoline, always use the hand guard. The amounts below fill roughly two quart jars, depending on how firmly you pack them.

| Ingredient | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Green cabbage, cored and very thinly shredded | 1 small head, about 2 pounds |
| Carrots, cut into thin matchsticks or coarsely grated | 2 medium |
| Red onion or shallots, thinly sliced | 1 small onion or 2 shallots |
| Red or green bell pepper, cut in thin strips | 1/2 pepper |
| Scotch bonnet peppers (piman bouk), thinly sliced | 2 to 4, or 1 seeded for mild |
| Garlic cloves, thinly sliced | 4 |
| Whole cloves | 6 |
| Black peppercorns | 1 teaspoon |
| Fine salt | 1 1/2 teaspoons |
| Distilled white vinegar labeled 5% acidity | 3 to 4 cups, enough to cover |
| Fresh lime juice (optional) | Juice of 1 lime |

### Choosing your heat

Is pikliz spicy? Traditional pikliz is very spicy, because scotch bonnets are fiery little peppers and close cousins of the habanero. Much of their heat sits in the pale inner ribs and the seeds, so removing them tames the jar a great deal. For a gentle family batch, use one scotch bonnet with the seeds and ribs removed, and let the jar sit a day before tasting.

If you want pikliz without scotch bonnet, a habanero is the closest stand in, with similar fruity heat. For a truly mild jar that children can enjoy, use a seeded jalapeño or simply leave the hot pepper out and add a little extra black pepper. You can always slip another sliced pepper into the jar later, but you cannot take heat back out once it is there.

### Method

- Wash and prep : Wash hands, rinse vegetables, and shred everything thin
- Gloves on : Slice the hot peppers wearing gloves
- Toss : Mix vegetables with salt, garlic, cloves, and peppercorns
- Pack and cover : Pack into clean jars and pour in vinegar to cover
- Chill : Refrigerate right away and wait at least one day

Start by washing your hands and rinsing the cabbage, carrots, onion, and peppers under running water. Shred and slice everything into a large clean bowl, then put on gloves before you cut the scotch bonnets. Add the hot peppers, garlic, cloves, peppercorns, and salt, and toss well with a clean spoon or with your gloved hands until the colors are evenly mixed.

Pack the vegetables into clean glass jars, pressing down gently so they settle. Pour in the vinegar until every shred is fully covered, add the lime juice if you are using it, and slide a clean spoon down the sides to release any air bubbles. Close the jars with clean lids and place them in the refrigerator right away. After about a day the pikliz is ready, and after two or three days the flavors deepen and the heat spreads through the whole jar.

## Keeping pikliz safe and crisp

### Handling hot peppers

The burning oil in hot peppers is called capsaicin, and it does not wash off easily. Poison Control advises wearing rubber, latex, or nitrile gloves when working with hot peppers and not touching your face or eyes afterward. If pepper does get into your eyes, they recommend rinsing with plenty of warm water for about fifteen minutes. If someone has trouble breathing or chest discomfort, call 911, and for other questions you can reach Poison Control at 1 800 222 1222.

### Clean jars, cold fridge, clean spoons

FoodSafety.gov recommends washing cutting boards, utensils, and countertops with hot, soapy water and rinsing produce under running water without soap. It also says your refrigerator should be set to 40°F or below, and that perishable foods should be refrigerated within two hours. That matters for pikliz, which has no cooking step to protect it. Always serve from the jar with a clean, dry spoon, never with a fork that has touched someone's plate, and keep the vegetables pushed down under the vinegar.

The vinegar matters too. The National Center for Home Food Preservation's refrigerator pickle lesson calls for vinegar of 5% acidity. We use the vinegar full strength and do not water it down. Look for the acidity on the label before you buy.

### How long does pikliz last?

Oregon State University's Food Hero refrigerator pickled vegetables recipe says to store the jars only in the refrigerator and to use them within three months. The National Center for Home Food Preservation gives the same three month window for its refrigerator pickles. Those are tested recipes, and ours is a home recipe, so we suggest enjoying your pikliz within about a month, when it is also at its crunchiest. If you ever see mold, a slimy texture, or an off smell, throw the whole jar away.

**Pikliz food safety at a glance**
- Wear gloves to cut hot peppers and keep hands away from eyes
- Use clean jars, lids, bowls, and spoons
- Use vinegar labeled 5% acidity at full strength
- Keep vegetables under the vinegar and the jar at 40°F or colder
- Store only in the refrigerator, never on the pantry shelf
- Enjoy within about a month and discard if anything looks or smells wrong

## What to eat with pikliz

So what do you eat with pikliz? In Haiti it is famously served beside fried dishes, but it shines with plant based foods too. Spoon it next to banann peze, the twice fried green plantains, or over a warm plate of diri ak pwa. It is wonderful tucked into a sandwich with black bean patties, served alongside baked sweet potatoes, or stirred into a simple bowl of brown rice and greens.

Related: [Diri ak Pwa the Healthy Way](https://shekinahsda.org/blog/diri-ak-pwa-the-healthy-way/)

### For the Thanksgiving table

Thanksgiving tables are often heavy with soft, rich foods, and pikliz offers exactly what they need: crunch, acid, and a little fire. A small bowl beside the stuffing, sweet potatoes, and plant based mains lets each guest add as much as they like. If you are carrying it to a family gathering, keep the jar in a cooler and put leftovers back in the refrigerator within two hours. Consider bringing one mild jar and one spicy jar, clearly marked, so nobody gets surprised.

## Good food for the body God gave us

Cabbage is a humble vegetable with a lot to offer. North Carolina State Extension notes that one cup of raw green cabbage has about 22 calories and 2 grams of fiber and provides 36% of the daily value for vitamin C. Harvard's Nutrition Source lists cruciferous vegetables like cabbage, along with bell peppers, among good food sources of vitamin C, and notes that high heat and long cooking can break the vitamin down. Pikliz is never cooked, though the exact nutrients in a finished jar will vary, so think of it as a flavorful way to eat more vegetables rather than a health food with promised numbers.

Our Seventh-day Adventist Fundamental Belief 22, Christian Behavior, reminds us that our bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit and that we should care for them intelligently, adopting the most healthful diet possible. That is not a call to bland food. Pikliz shows how a few vegetables, a little salt, and good vinegar can make a plate both nourishing and full of joy. Because it does contain salt, a spoonful or two at a time is plenty.

## Flavor, salt, and the goodness of God

Scripture often uses taste to teach us about God. David wrote a psalm of praise that invites everyone to experience God's goodness for themselves. It is one of the warmest invitations in the whole Bible.

> "O taste and see that the LORD is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him." Psalm 34:8, KJV

David was not writing about food, but he chose the language of taste because some things must be experienced to be understood. Jesus did something similar when He told His followers, "Ye are the salt of the earth" (Matthew 5:13), and Paul urged believers to let their speech be "alway with grace, seasoned with salt" (Colossians 4:6). Just as a little pikliz brightens an entire plate, a life touched by Christ can bring warmth and flavor to the people around it. These are pictures, not recipes, yet they remind us that even our ordinary meals can point us to the One who made every good thing.

## Questions people ask

### What is pikliz made of?

Pikliz is made of thinly shredded cabbage, carrots, onion, bell pepper, garlic, and hot scotch bonnet peppers, covered in vinegar and left to steep in the refrigerator. Our Shekinah style recipe also adds whole cloves, black peppercorns, salt, and an optional squeeze of fresh lime juice. Researchers writing in the Journal of Ethnic Foods describe pikliz as shredded cabbage and carrot with plenty of hot pepper and spices immersed in vinegar or lemon juice. For safety and flavor, use distilled white vinegar labeled 5% acidity at full strength.

### Is pikliz spicy?

Traditional pikliz is very spicy, because it is made with scotch bonnet peppers, called piman bouk in Kreyòl, which are close cousins of the habanero. Much of the heat sits in the pale inner ribs and the seeds, so removing them tames the jar a great deal. For a mild family batch, use one seeded scotch bonnet or a seeded jalapeño, or leave the hot pepper out and add a little extra black pepper. You can always slip more pepper into the jar later, but you cannot take heat back out.

### Do you have to refrigerate pikliz?

Yes, homemade pikliz must always be kept in the refrigerator at 40°F or colder, because it is a refrigerator pickle and never a shelf stable canned product. FoodSafety.gov recommends setting your refrigerator to 40°F or below and refrigerating perishable foods within two hours. Oregon State University's Food Hero recipe for refrigerator pickled vegetables also says to store the jars only in the refrigerator. Keep the vegetables pushed under the vinegar and always serve with a clean, dry spoon.

### How soon can you eat pikliz after making it?

Pikliz is ready to eat after about one day in the refrigerator, and it tastes even better after two or three days. During that time the vinegar soaks into the thin shreds of cabbage and carrot, the flavors deepen, and the heat of the scotch bonnets spreads through the whole jar. Slicing the cabbage as thin as you can helps it absorb the vinegar while staying pleasantly crisp. For the best crunch, enjoy a homemade jar within about a month.

## Reflection questions

When you share a meal this week, how could you make room for gratitude before the first bite? Who in your life might need the kind of encouragement that brightens a hard day, the way pikliz brightens a plate? And as Thanksgiving approaches, what simple dish could you prepare and share as an act of kindness for a neighbor or someone eating alone?

## A word of encouragement

You do not need to be a perfect cook to bless your family. A jar of pikliz takes about thirty minutes of chopping and a little patience, yet it can carry the taste of home to a homesick friend or welcome a guest to your table. God sees the care you put into everyday things, and nothing done in love is ever small. As you slice, pack, and share, may your kitchen become a place where people feel at home and taste His goodness.

## A prayer

Lord, thank You for the gift of food and for the simple things that make our tables bright. Thank You for cabbage and carrots, for peppers and spices, and for the hands that prepare them. Help us care for the bodies You have given us, and make our lives a seasoning of grace to everyone we meet. We ask this in the name of Jesus, amen.

After the service our church family shares a meal together, and there is always room for one more at the table. Visit our Plan Your Visit page to learn what to expect.

- Source: [Valorization of pikliz: a spicy meal garnishment in Haitian cuisine, Journal of Ethnic Foods](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s42779-021-00077-5)

- Source: [Capsaicin: When the chili is too hot, Poison Control](https://www.poison.org/articles/capsaicin-when-the-chili-is-too-hot)

- Source: [4 Steps to Food Safety, FoodSafety.gov](https://www.foodsafety.gov/keep-food-safe/4-steps-to-food-safety)

- Source: [Refrigerator Pickled Vegetables, Oregon State University Extension Food Hero](https://extension.oregonstate.edu/node/175386)

- Source: [Refrigerator Pickles, National Center for Home Food Preservation](https://newt.fcs.uga.edu/nchfp/putitup/Poster%203%20Beginning%20(Refrigerator%20Pickles).pdf)

- Source: [We All Need to Eat Cabbage, NC State Extension](https://beaufort.ces.ncsu.edu/2025/02/we-all-need-to-eat-cabbage)

> "O taste and see that the LORD is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him." Psalm 34:8, KJV

# Sunlight in the Shorter Days: Vitamin D, Mood, and God's Gift of Light

URL: https://shekinahsda.org/blog/sunlight-in-the-shorter-days-vitamin-d-and-mood/
Category: Health
Author: Claire Benson
Published: 2026-10-26

As fall and winter days grow shorter, trusted health sources explain how sunlight, food, and medical care support vitamin D and mood, while Scripture reminds us that light is a good gift from God.


You leave for work and the sky is still gray. By the time you head home, the porch light is already on and supper is waiting in a dark kitchen. Many of us notice that our energy drops and our mood dips as the days shorten. If you have wondered whether that is more than your imagination, you are asking a good question.

Light is one of the first gifts God spoke into the world, and our bodies were made to respond to it. Sunlight helps the skin make vitamin D, it sets the rhythm of our sleep and waking, and for some people the loss of daylight is tied to real changes in mood. At the same time, too much sun carries its own risks, and not every skin type makes vitamin D the same way.

Below we look at what trusted health sources say about vitamin D in winter, plant based food sources, and seasonal mood changes. Then we open the Scriptures on light, keeping medical facts and spiritual lessons clearly separate. This is general wellness education, not medical advice, so please talk with your doctor about your own needs.

## The short answer

- 600 IU : Daily vitamin D RDA for ages 1 to 70 (NIH)
- 800 IU : Daily RDA for adults 71 and older (NIH)
- None : Vitamin D your skin makes from sun through a window (NIH)

Your body makes vitamin D when bare skin is exposed to the sun, and the National Institutes of Health notes that most people get at least some vitamin D this way. In fall and winter that becomes harder, because days are shorter, we spend more time indoors, and sunlight through a window does not count. The NIH Office of Dietary Supplements sets the Recommended Dietary Allowance at 600 IU (15 mcg) a day for most children and adults, and 800 IU (20 mcg) for adults over 70. Food can help close the gap, but the only reliable way to know your own level is a blood test ordered by your doctor.

Low mood in the darker months deserves attention too. Feeling a little sluggish is common, but seasonal affective disorder is a real form of depression. If sadness lingers, interferes with daily life, or includes thoughts of self harm, please reach out for professional help right away.

## How sunlight helps your body make vitamin D

Vitamin D is a nutrient your body needs for strong bones, and the NIH explains that it helps your body absorb calcium. Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health calls vitamin D production in the skin the primary natural source of the vitamin. That process depends on a type of ultraviolet light called UVB reaching your skin, and Harvard notes that window glass completely blocks it. So a sunny room feels pleasant, but it does not raise your vitamin D level.

The NIH adds that clouds, smog, older age, and darker skin all reduce the amount of vitamin D your skin makes. Sunscreen matters as well, since Harvard reports that correctly applied sunscreen can reduce vitamin D absorption by more than 90 percent. Season and location also change how strong UVB rays are. Harvard gives the example that people in Boston cannot make enough vitamin D from sunlight for about 4 months of the year. North Texas sits much farther south, so our winter sun is stronger, but shorter days and long hours indoors still add up.

### How much sun do you need for vitamin D?

The honest answer is that no single number fits everyone. Harvard notes that the amount of vitamin D the skin makes varies widely, depending on skin tone, age, season, location, and sunscreen use. Skin doctors also urge caution. The American Academy of Dermatology states that unprotected exposure to the sun's ultraviolet rays is a known risk factor for skin cancer, and it recommends that healthy adults get their vitamin D from food rather than from sun exposure or tanning. The wise path is to enjoy daylight while avoiding sunburn, and to rely on food and your doctor for vitamin D itself.

## Darker skin and vitamin D: a word for Haitian families

Many families in our church have roots in Haiti, so this matters for us. The NIH puts it plainly: the darker your skin, the less vitamin D you make from sunlight exposure. Harvard explains that melanin, the pigment that gives skin its color, acts like a shade and reduces vitamin D production. Harvard also cites United States data showing that about 20 percent of White adults and about 75 percent of Black adults have blood levels of vitamin D below 50 nmol/L. This is not a reason for worry or shame, since the variety of skin God created is part of His design, but it is a good reason to ask your doctor about a vitamin D blood test, especially in winter.

Darker skin does not mean sun protection can be skipped, since the sun safety advice from health agencies is written for everyone. The CDC advises protecting your skin all year long by staying in the shade during midday hours, wearing clothing that covers your arms and legs, and using sunscreen with SPF 15 or higher that protects against both UVA and UVB rays. The goal for every family is balance: get outside, avoid burning, and pay attention to vitamin D through food and medical guidance.

**Who may need extra attention to vitamin D (NIH)**
- Breastfed infants
- Older adults
- People who rarely get sun exposure
- People with darker skin
- People with conditions that limit fat absorption
- People with obesity or past gastric bypass surgery

## How much vitamin D do you need?

The NIH Office of Dietary Supplements lists daily recommended amounts by age, counting vitamin D from all foods, beverages, and supplements together. These are a general guide for healthy people. Your doctor may advise differently based on your health and your blood test.

| Age group | Recommended daily amount (NIH) |
| --- | --- |
| Birth to 12 months | 10 mcg (400 IU) |
| Children and teens, 1 to 18 years | 15 mcg (600 IU) |
| Adults, 19 to 70 years | 15 mcg (600 IU) |
| Adults 71 years and older | 20 mcg (800 IU) |
| Pregnant and breastfeeding | 15 mcg (600 IU) |

More is not always better. The NIH warns that getting too much vitamin D can be harmful, and that extremely high levels can cause kidney failure, irregular heartbeat, and even death. Please do not start high dose supplements on your own, and tell your doctor or pharmacist about any supplement you take.

## Vitamin D foods for a plant based kitchen

Many Seventh-day Adventists eat a plant based or vegetarian diet, and this is where vitamin D needs a little planning. Harvard notes that people who do not eat milk, eggs, or fish, such as those following a vegan diet, are at higher risk of low vitamin D. Fortified foods do most of the work.

The NIH notes that almost all of the United States milk supply is fortified with about 3 mcg (120 IU) of vitamin D per cup, and that many plant based alternatives such as soy milk, almond milk, and oat milk are similarly fortified. Check the label, because fortification varies by brand. The NIH also explains that some mushrooms have been exposed to ultraviolet light to increase their vitamin D content.

In a Haitian kitchen this can look very natural. Oatmeal made with fortified soy or oat milk, or mushrooms folded into a vegetable legim beside your diri ak pwa, are simple ways to bring vitamin D foods to the table. If your diet still leaves you short, ask your doctor whether a supplement makes sense for you.

## Morning light, sleep, and mood

Sunlight also shapes our daily rhythm. The National Institute of General Medical Sciences explains that circadian rhythms are the changes our bodies go through over a 24 hour cycle, and that light and dark have the biggest influence on them. In the evening, the brain's master clock signals the body to make more melatonin, which causes sleepiness.

NIGMS also notes that light from electronic devices at night can confuse our biological clocks. A short walk after breakfast, opening the curtains wide, or eating lunch outdoors on a mild Texas afternoon are gentle ways to give your body clear signals about day and night. Dimming screens in the evening completes the picture.

Related: [The Gift of Rest: Why Sleep Is Part of Our Worship](https://shekinahsda.org/blog/the-gift-of-rest-why-sleep-is-part-of-our-worship/)

## Winter blues or seasonal affective disorder?

Feeling a bit down when daylight shrinks is often called the winter blues. Seasonal affective disorder is different. NIMH describes it as a type of depression with a recurring seasonal pattern. Symptoms usually begin in late fall or early winter, ease in spring and summer, and last about 4 to 5 months a year.

According to NIMH, the winter pattern can include oversleeping, overeating with cravings for carbohydrates, weight gain, and pulling away from other people. Mayo Clinic adds low energy and notes that possible causes include reduced sunlight disrupting the body's internal clock, a drop in serotonin, and shifts in melatonin. It is diagnosed more often in women than in men and occurs more often in younger adults, and Mayo Clinic lists a low level of vitamin D among the risk factors.

There is real help available. NIMH describes four main types of treatment: light therapy, talk therapy, antidepressant medicine, and vitamin D. For light therapy, people typically sit in front of a special 10,000 lux light box for about 30 to 45 minutes a day, usually in the morning, and NIMH notes that vitamin D supplements may help some people, although studies have shown mixed results. These choices belong with a health professional.

**When to reach out for help**
- Low mood that lasts for days and steals your joy
- Changes in sleep or appetite that will not settle
- Feeling hopeless or withdrawing from people
- Any thoughts of self harm or suicide: call or text 988 now

Mayo Clinic advises seeing a health care provider when you feel down for days at a time and lose motivation for activities you usually enjoy, especially if sleep or appetite change. If you or someone you love is struggling or having thoughts of suicide, NIMH points to the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, which you can call or text at 988 in the United States. Asking for help is not a lack of faith but wisdom, and it is one way God brings healing through caring people.

## What the Bible says about light

The Bible is not a nutrition textbook, and we should not read vitamin D into its pages. What Scripture gives us instead is a picture of light as a good gift from a loving Creator. Light was part of His design from the very first day.

> "And God said, Let there be light: and there was light." Genesis 1:3, KJV

The next verse adds that "God saw the light, that it was good" (Genesis 1:4). Later in the same chapter God set lights in the sky "to divide the day from the night" (Genesis 1:14), giving our days and seasons their rhythm. The wise teacher of Ecclesiastes delighted in this gift, writing, "Truly the light is sweet, and a pleasant thing it is for the eyes to behold the sun" (Ecclesiastes 11:7). In the next verse he also tells us to remember "the days of darkness; for they shall be many" (Ecclesiastes 11:8), an honest admission that life includes darker seasons alongside the bright ones.

### The Sun of righteousness and the Light of the world

Malachi used the image of sunrise to describe God's coming salvation, and Christians have long understood this promise as pointing to the Messiah. This is a spiritual picture, not a medical claim. Still, it speaks deeply to anyone walking through a gray season.

> "But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall." Malachi 4:2, KJV

Jesus made the image personal when He said, "I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life" (John 8:12). The light our bodies need comes from the sun God made, but the light our souls need comes from the Son God sent. Both are gifts, and we are invited to receive both with gratitude.

## Sunlight and the eight natural remedies

Seventh-day Adventists often speak of eight natural remedies for health: nutrition, exercise, water, sunlight, temperance, fresh air, rest, and trust in God. Sunlight is on that list, and so is temperance. Together they remind us that even good gifts are best enjoyed with balance, which is exactly the lesson of sun and skin.

The church's Fundamental Belief 22, Christian Behavior, teaches that "because our bodies are the temples of the Holy Spirit, we are to care for them intelligently." Paul asked the believers in Corinth, "know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you" (1 Corinthians 6:19). Caring wisely for our bodies in winter, through food, daylight, rest, and medical care when needed, is one small way to honor the God who made us.

- Step outside early : Take a short walk or sit outdoors in the morning light
- Check your milk : Choose a plant milk labeled as fortified with vitamin D
- Add mushrooms : Look for UV treated mushrooms at the store
- Protect your skin : Seek shade at midday and avoid sunburn
- Talk to your doctor : Ask about a vitamin D blood test before supplementing

## Questions people ask

### Can you get vitamin D through a window?

No, you cannot get vitamin D from sunlight that comes through a window, because window glass completely blocks the UVB rays your skin needs to make it, as the Harvard School of Public Health explains. A bright, sunny room may lift your spirits, but it does not raise your vitamin D level. To make vitamin D, bare skin needs direct sun outdoors. Even then, the American Academy of Dermatology recommends that healthy adults get their vitamin D from food rather than from sun exposure.

### Does darker skin make less vitamin D?

Yes, darker skin makes less vitamin D from sunlight, and the NIH states plainly that the darker your skin, the less vitamin D you make from sun exposure. Harvard explains that melanin, the pigment that gives skin its color, acts like a shade and reduces vitamin D production. Harvard also cites United States data showing that about 75 percent of Black adults have vitamin D blood levels below 50 nmol/L, compared with about 20 percent of White adults. That is a good reason for Haitian families and anyone with darker skin to ask a doctor about a vitamin D blood test, especially in winter.

### What plant based foods have vitamin D?

The main plant based sources of vitamin D are fortified foods, such as soy milk, almond milk, and oat milk labeled as fortified, along with mushrooms that have been exposed to ultraviolet light. The NIH notes that many plant milks are fortified much like cow's milk, which carries about 3 mcg (120 IU) per cup, but fortification varies by brand, so check the label. Harvard notes that people following a vegan diet are at higher risk of low vitamin D, so this takes a little planning. Oatmeal made with fortified soy or oat milk, or mushrooms folded into a vegetable legim, are simple ways to bring these foods to a Haitian table.

### Is low vitamin D linked to seasonal affective disorder?

Low vitamin D is linked to seasonal affective disorder, since Mayo Clinic lists a low level of vitamin D among its risk factors, but a risk factor is not proof that it causes the condition. Mayo Clinic also points to reduced sunlight disrupting the body's internal clock, a drop in serotonin, and shifts in melatonin as possible causes. The National Institute of Mental Health includes vitamin D among four main types of treatment, while noting that studies of vitamin D supplements have shown mixed results. If low mood lasts for days or steals your joy, please talk with a health care provider, and call or text 988 if you have any thoughts of self harm.

## Reflection questions

Take these questions with you on a Sabbath afternoon walk. When you think about the darker seasons of your own life, where have you seen the light of Christ break through? What is one simple change you could make this winter to welcome more of God's daylight into your routine? Is there someone in your family or church who seems to be struggling as the days grow short, and how might you reach out to them with kindness?

## A word of encouragement

If the shorter days have left you feeling heavy, you are not weak and you are not alone. God made our bodies to respond to light, so it makes sense that we feel the change when it fades. He has also given us food, rest, doctors, and a church family to help us through.

Every winter gives way to spring, and the psalmist wrote, "weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning" (Psalm 30:5). Whatever season you are in, the Light of the world walks with you. His mercy has not grown dim.

## A prayer

Father, thank You for the sun that warms our days and for the rhythm of seasons You set in motion. When the days grow short and our hearts feel heavy, help us to care wisely for the bodies You have given us. Shine the light of Jesus into every dark place in our lives, and give us courage to ask for help when we need it. In Jesus' name, Amen.

## Your next step

If this season has been heavy, our church family would be honored to pray with you, so please share a prayer request. You are also warmly invited to join us for Sabbath School at 10:00 AM and Divine Service at 11:00 AM at 205 E Carver St in Alvarado, Texas, where we worship in Kreyòl and English. After the service we share a meal together, and there is always a place at the table for you.
