# The Gift of Rest: Why Sleep Is Part of Our Worship

URL: https://shekinahsda.org/blog/the-gift-of-rest-why-sleep-is-part-of-our-worship/
Category: Health
Author: Samuel Brooks
Published: 2026-09-28

Health experts say most adults need at least seven hours of sleep, and Scripture shows that receiving rest is an act of trust in the God who watches over us.


It is almost midnight, and the house is finally quiet. The dishes are done, the children are asleep, and you tell yourself you will rest right after a few more messages. Then the clock says one in the morning, your mind is still racing about tomorrow, and you wonder why you feel so tired all the time. If that sounds familiar, you are far from alone.

Many of us treat sleep as the first thing to cut when life gets full, and we quietly feel that going to bed early is a kind of laziness. Yet Scripture tells a different story. From the first week of Creation to the ministry of Jesus, the Bible presents rest not as weakness but as a gift from a loving Creator who knows exactly how we are made.

In this article we will look at what health experts say about how much sleep adults need, what the Bible teaches about sleep and trust, and why Seventh-day Adventists see caring for our bodies as part of our worship. Along the way you will find simple, practical habits for sleeping better tonight. This is general health education, not medical advice, so if you struggle with sleep often, please talk with your doctor.

## The short answer

- 7 hours : Minimum nightly sleep the CDC recommends for adults 18 to 60
- 1 in 3 : US adults who report not getting enough rest or sleep every day (NHLBI)
- 30 minutes : Wind down time before bed suggested by the Sleep Foundation

Most adults need at least seven hours of sleep each night. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends seven or more hours for adults ages 18 to 60, and the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute notes that experts recommend between seven and nine hours a night for adults. Adults who regularly sleep fewer than seven hours may face more health problems than those who get enough.

Spiritually, the Bible invites us to see sleep as an act of trust. When we lie down and close our eyes, we admit that we cannot hold the world together by ourselves. God does not need us to stay awake in order to keep His promises, and He gives rest to His children as a gift. Sleep, received with gratitude, becomes a small daily surrender into His care.

## How much sleep do adults really need?

Sleep needs change across a lifetime. Children and teenagers need more sleep than adults, and older adults still need about seven to eight hours. The CDC publishes these ranges for each age group, a helpful guide for families setting bedtimes.

| Age group | Recommended sleep (CDC) |
| --- | --- |
| School age, 6 to 12 years | 9 to 12 hours |
| Teens, 13 to 17 years | 8 to 10 hours |
| Adults, 18 to 60 years | 7 or more hours |
| Adults, 61 to 64 years | 7 to 9 hours |
| Adults, 65 and older | 7 to 8 hours |

Those numbers can feel out of reach when you work long shifts, but the gap matters. The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute reports that about one in three adults in the United States say they do not get enough rest or sleep every day. It also links ongoing sleep deficiency to heart disease, high blood pressure, diabetes, stroke, obesity, and depression, along with a higher risk of injury from accidents such as drowsy driving.

The CDC describes the other side of the picture as well. Getting enough sleep can help you get sick less often, stay at a healthy weight, lower your risk for serious conditions such as type 2 diabetes and heart disease, reduce stress, improve your mood, and sharpen your attention and memory. Sleep is not wasted time but the hidden work that makes the rest of your day possible.

## What the Bible says about sleep

The Bible does not give us a sleep schedule, and we should be careful not to read modern science into ancient texts. What Scripture does give us is a picture of God as the One who watches over us while we rest. It also offers a gentle correction for the anxious striving that keeps so many of us awake.

### Sleep as an act of trust

David wrote some of his most peaceful words during some of the most dangerous seasons of his life. Psalm 3 is titled as a psalm he wrote when he fled from his son Absalom, and yet he could say, "I laid me down and slept; I awaked; for the LORD sustained me" (Psalm 3:5). In the very next psalm, he expresses the same quiet confidence.

> "I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety." Psalm 4:8, KJV

Notice where David places his safety. It is not in his own watchfulness or his plans for the next day, but in the Lord alone. When we lie awake replaying every worry, we are often carrying a weight God never asked us to carry through the night.

### The vanity of anxious overwork

Psalm 127 speaks directly to the habit of burning the candle at both ends. This psalm, whose title links it to Solomon, reminds us that unless the Lord builds the house, the builders labor in vain. Then he adds a striking line about sleep.

> "It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep." Psalm 127:2, KJV

This verse does not condemn hard work, which Scripture honors in many places. It warns against the anxious, sorrowful toil that believes everything depends on us. The phrase "he giveth his beloved sleep" turns sleep into a love gift. God gives rest to the people He loves, and receiving that rest is one way of trusting His love.

## Elijah under the juniper tree

One of the most tender stories about rest in Scripture comes from the life of Elijah. After a dramatic victory on Mount Carmel, he received a death threat from Queen Jezebel and fled into the wilderness. Exhausted and discouraged, he sat under a juniper tree and asked God to take his life (1 Kings 19:4).

What God did next is beautiful. He did not lecture Elijah or tell him to pray harder. He let him sleep, and then He fed him.

> "And as he lay and slept under a juniper tree, behold, then an angel touched him, and said unto him, Arise and eat. And he looked, and, behold, there was a cake baken on the coals, and a cruse of water at his head. And he did eat and drink, and laid him down again." 1 Kings 19:5 to 6, KJV

The angel came a second time and said, "Arise and eat; because the journey is too great for thee" (1 Kings 19:7). Elijah then went in the strength of that food for forty days and forty nights to Horeb, the mount of God (1 Kings 19:8). Only after his body had been cared for did God speak to him in the still small voice. The order matters, and it is a gentle lesson for weary believers.

**What God gave Elijah**
- Sleep, more than once
- Simple food and water
- A gentle touch, not a rebuke
- Honest words about the journey ahead
- Then, a quiet word from God Himself

## Jesus invites tired disciples to rest

The same compassion shows up in the ministry of Jesus. After the disciples returned from a busy season of preaching and healing, crowds were pressing in from every side. Mark tells us they did not even have time to eat. Jesus noticed, and He made rest a priority.

> "And he said unto them, Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while: for there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat." Mark 6:31, KJV

Jesus did not see rest as a distraction from ministry but as part of faithful living. The Savior who said, "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28), also knew that tired bodies need real sleep. If Jesus called His closest friends to rest, we can stop feeling guilty when our bodies ask for the same.

## Why Adventists see sleep as part of worship

Seventh-day Adventists believe that our bodies are a gift from God and that caring for them is part of how we honor Him. The church's Fundamental Belief 22, Christian Behavior, calls believers to live in harmony with biblical principles and includes adequate rest alongside exercise and a healthful diet. Paul put the principle simply: "whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God" (1 Corinthians 10:31). That includes how we sleep.

Many Adventist churches teach eight natural remedies for health: good nutrition, exercise, water, sunlight, temperance, fresh air, rest, and trust in God. Rest and trust sit side by side on that list for a reason. Most of us cannot truly rest until we trust, and sleep is often the first place where our faith or our fear shows up.

The weekly Sabbath carries this principle further. Fundamental Belief 20 describes it as "a day of delightful communion with God and one another" and "the day of rest, worship, and ministry," kept from sunset to sunset. Nightly sleep restores the body day by day, while the Sabbath restores the whole person week by week, a rhythm God built into creation.

Related: [Resting in His Presence: What the Sabbath Teaches Us About Trust](https://shekinahsda.org/blog/resting-in-his-presence-what-the-sabbath-teaches-us-about-trust/)

## Practical ways to sleep better

Good intentions are not enough on their own, and most of us need a few simple habits that make sleep easier to receive. The suggestions below come from the CDC, Mayo Clinic, and the Sleep Foundation. None of them require special equipment.

### Keep a steady schedule

The CDC and Mayo Clinic both recommend going to bed and getting up at the same time each day, including weekends. A regular rhythm helps your body know when it is time to wind down. Mayo Clinic also suggests that if you cannot fall asleep within about 20 minutes, you get up and do something relaxing until you feel tired, rather than lying in bed frustrated.

### Prepare your room and your evening

Keep your bedroom quiet, dark, relaxing, and cool. The CDC advises turning off electronics at least 30 minutes before bed, and the Sleep Foundation suggests building in a 30 to 60 minute device free buffer before sleep, since screens keep the mind stimulated. It also recommends setting aside about 30 minutes to wind down with calming activities such as soft music, light stretching, or reading.

### Watch evening food, drink, and activity

The CDC recommends avoiding large meals and alcohol before bed and avoiding caffeine in the afternoon or evening. Adventists already avoid alcohol and many avoid caffeine altogether, and that choice can be a quiet blessing for sleep. Daytime activity helps too, since the Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans note that it can improve sleep quality, and Mayo Clinic suggests avoiding being active too close to bedtime.

### Lay your worries down before you lie down

Mayo Clinic recommends settling concerns before bed, for example by writing them down and setting them aside for tomorrow. For a believer, that list can become a prayer. Writing down what weighs on you and placing it before God is a practical way to obey Peter's counsel to cast all your care upon Him, because He cares for you (1 Peter 5:7).

- Set a bedtime : Choose a time that allows at least seven hours
- Screens off : Put devices away 30 to 60 minutes before bed
- Dim the room : Keep it quiet, dark, and cool
- Pray your worries : Write them down and give them to God
- Read and rest : Close with a psalm, then lights out

### Know when to see a doctor

An occasional sleepless night is normal. If trouble sleeping happens often, though, Mayo Clinic advises contacting your health care provider so that any underlying cause can be found and treated. The NHLBI notes that an estimated 50 to 70 million Americans have chronic sleep disorders, so asking for help is common and wise. Seeing a doctor about sleep is not a lack of faith. It is good stewardship of the body God gave you.

## A word for families and busy households

In many Haitian homes, evenings are full and lively, with food to prepare, family calling from Haiti, and homework to check. Yet children and teens need even more sleep than adults, so a household rhythm that protects bedtime is one of the kindest gifts parents can give. A short family worship with a song in Kreyòl or English, a psalm, and a prayer can signal that the day is closing. It also teaches children that we fall asleep in the care of a God who never sleeps, because "he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep" (Psalm 121:4).

## Questions people ask

### Is going to bed early a sign of laziness?

Going to bed early is not laziness, because the Bible presents rest as a gift from a loving Creator rather than a weakness. Psalm 127:2 warns against the anxious habit of rising early and sitting up late, and it says that God "giveth his beloved sleep." That verse does not condemn hard work, which Scripture honors in many places, but it reminds us that everything does not depend on us. Choosing a bedtime that allows at least seven hours, as the CDC recommends for adults 18 to 60, is a wise way to receive the rest God offers.

### What Bible verse can I pray when I cannot sleep?

Psalm 4:8 is one of the best Bible verses to pray when you cannot sleep: "I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety." David also wrote in Psalm 3:5 that he laid down and slept and awoke because the Lord sustained him. Psalm 121:4 reminds us that the One who keeps Israel never slumbers nor sleeps, so we can rest while He keeps watch. You can also write down what weighs on you and give it to God, following Peter's counsel in 1 Peter 5:7 to cast all your care upon Him.

### What should I do if I cannot fall asleep after 20 minutes?

If you cannot fall asleep within about 20 minutes, Mayo Clinic suggests getting up and doing something relaxing until you feel tired, rather than lying in bed frustrated. Keep the lights low and the room quiet, dark, and cool so your body still knows it is time to wind down. This is a good moment to read a psalm or quietly pray through what is on your mind. A steady bedtime and wake time each day, including weekends, also helps your body settle into a healthy rhythm over time.

### Is seeing a doctor about sleep problems a lack of faith?

Seeing a doctor about sleep problems is not a lack of faith but good stewardship of the body God gave you. Mayo Clinic advises contacting your health care provider if trouble sleeping happens often, so that any underlying cause can be found and treated. The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute estimates that 50 to 70 million Americans have chronic sleep disorders, so asking for help is common and wise. Seventh-day Adventists believe caring for our bodies is part of how we honor God, and that includes getting good care when we need it.

## Reflection questions

Take a quiet moment with these questions tonight, perhaps before you turn off the light. What is one habit that regularly keeps you up later than you intend, and what would it look like to hand that time back to God? When you lie awake worrying, what would change if you truly believed that God keeps watch while you sleep? How might your family protect bedtime as a gift instead of treating it as something to squeeze in when everything else is done?

## A word of encouragement

If you have been running on empty, hear this gently: you are not a failure for being tired. Elijah was tired, the disciples were tired, and God met them with food, sleep, and kindness before He gave them their next assignment. He is the same God today, and He knows your frame and remembers that you are dust (Psalm 103:14).

Start small by choosing one habit from this article and trying it for a week. Go to bed a little earlier or pray through your worries on paper. Each time you lie down in peace, you are telling God that you trust Him, and that simple act of trust is a beautiful form of worship.

## A prayer

Father, thank You for the gift of sleep and for watching over me through every night. Forgive me for the times I have carried burdens You never asked me to carry. Teach me to lie down in peace and to trust You with tomorrow. Restore my body, quiet my mind, and let my rest bring glory to You. In Jesus' name, Amen.

## Your next step

If worry or weariness has been keeping you awake, you do not have to carry it alone. Our church family would be honored to pray with you, so share a prayer request below. We also meet for prayer on Zoom every Tuesday and Wednesday at 7:30 PM, and you are always welcome to join us.

# Soup Joumou, Plant Based: A Freedom Tradition for the Whole Table

URL: https://shekinahsda.org/blog/soup-joumou-plant-based-a-freedom-tradition-for-the-whole-table/
Category: Recipes
Author: Marie Laurent
Published: 2026-09-21

The story of Haiti's freedom soup, from January 1, 1804 to UNESCO recognition, with a full plant based soup joumou recipe the whole table can share.


It is the last night of December, and somewhere a Haitian kitchen is already busy. The squash has been peeled and cubed, the epis is waiting in a jar, and a big pot is being pulled down from the top shelf because this soup is never made in small amounts. By morning, bowls will be passed to family, neighbors, and anyone who walks through the door. For many Haitians at home and around the world, the new year does not truly begin until the first spoonful of soup joumou.

Maybe you grew up with that tradition and want to keep it alive in a new country. Maybe you are married into a Haitian family and want to learn the soup your in laws talk about every January. Or maybe you follow a plant based diet and wonder whether a dish usually made with beef can still taste like celebration. Whatever brought you here, this soup is worth learning, because it carries a story of freedom that every one of us can understand.

In this article we will look at the history behind soup joumou, why UNESCO recognized it as part of the world's cultural heritage, and what the Bible says about the freedom it celebrates. Then we will walk through a full plant based soup joumou recipe, rich with squash, vegetables, pasta, and epis, with chickpeas standing in for the beef so the whole table can share one pot.

## The short answer

Soup joumou is a Haitian squash soup traditionally eaten on January 1, Haiti's Independence Day. Under French colonial rule it was reserved for slave owners, and after Haiti declared independence on January 1, 1804, Haitians claimed the soup as their own and made it a symbol of freedom and dignity. In 2021, UNESCO added it to its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

- 1804 : Year Haiti declared independence on January 1
- 2021 : Year UNESCO inscribed joumou soup
- 8 : Generous servings from one pot

A plant based version keeps everything that makes the soup special, the bright orange squash broth, the tender vegetables, the pasta, and the herb filled epis, while swapping the beef for chickpeas. The result is hearty, colorful, and fully in keeping with the Adventist health message, which encourages a balanced vegetarian diet with legumes, whole grains, fruits, and vegetables.

Chickpeas are a smart stand in for beef. Harvard's Nutrition Source describes legumes as a source of protein and both soluble and insoluble fiber, and notes that whole legumes are naturally low in saturated fat and sodium. They also hold their shape in a long simmer, so every spoonful gets a little something to bite into.

## The history of soup joumou

### A soup that was forbidden

During the colonial period, the land we now call Haiti was the French colony of Saint Domingue, and enslaved Africans did the brutal work of its plantations. According to UNESCO, joumou soup was originally reserved for slave owners. Al Jazeera's report on the UNESCO decision explains that enslaved Haitians prepared the soup but were never allowed to eat it themselves.

Think about what that means. People spent hours cutting, stirring, and seasoning a meal they could smell but never taste. The soup became a daily reminder of who was considered free and who was not.

### January 1, 1804

On January 1, 1804, in the port city of Gonaïves, Jean Jacques Dessalines proclaimed the independence of Haiti. Haiti became the first nation in Latin America and the Caribbean to win its independence, and the second in the Americas after the United States. It was also the first country to be founded by formerly enslaved people.

Haitians celebrated their freedom by eating the very soup that had been denied to them. What had been a symbol of exclusion became a symbol of liberty. To this day, soup joumou is eaten on New Year's Day to remember the revolution, and many families continue serving it on January 2, Ancestry Day, a holiday honoring the heroes of independence.

- Colonial era: A soup for slave owners: Enslaved people grow and cook the squash but are not allowed to eat the soup.

- January 1, 1804: Independence in Gonaïves: Dessalines proclaims Haiti free, and Haitians claim the soup as their own.

- Every January 1: The first meal of the year: Families share soup joumou to remember freedom and dignity.

- December 2021: Recognized by UNESCO: Joumou soup is added to the Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage.

### Recognized by the world

In December 2021, UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage committee inscribed joumou soup on its Representative List. It was Haiti's first inscription on the list. UNESCO describes the soup as a celebratory dish tied to Haitian identity, one that promotes social cohesion and a sense of belonging, and that became a symbol of the dignity and resilience of Haitians after independence.

UNESCO also notes that the soup is a traditional Sunday breakfast, not only a New Year's dish. The traditional ingredients it lists include giraumon pumpkin, vegetables, plantains, meat, pasta, and spices. Recipes vary from family to family, and every Haitian kitchen seems to have its own small secret.

## Freedom through the eyes of Scripture

The story of soup joumou echoes one of the oldest themes in the Bible. God revealed Himself to Israel as the One who brought them out of slavery in Egypt, and He gave them a weekly Sabbath in part to remember that freedom (Deuteronomy 5:15). Slaves never rest. Free people do.

The New Testament carries that theme even deeper. Jesus told the people listening to Him, "If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed" (John 8:36). He was speaking about a freedom no government can grant and no chain can take away, freedom from sin, guilt, and fear.

> "Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage." Galatians 5:1, KJV

Paul wrote these words to Christians who were tempted to trade the grace of Jesus for a life of trying to earn God's favor. His message was simple: you have been set free, so do not go back. A bowl of soup joumou can become a small sermon at the table, reminding us that the God who cares about justice for the oppressed also offers every person freedom through Jesus.

The psalmist adds an invitation that fits a festive meal perfectly: "O taste and see that the LORD is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him" (Psalm 34:8). The verse is about experiencing God's goodness personally, not about food, but there is something fitting about tasting a dish of freedom and remembering the One who sets us free.

Related: [Resting in His Presence: What the Sabbath Teaches Us About Trust](https://shekinahsda.org/blog/resting-in-his-presence-what-the-sabbath-teaches-us-about-trust/)

## Plant based soup joumou recipe

This recipe makes about 8 generous servings, enough for a family gathering or a week of lunches. Plan on about 30 minutes of prep and about 1 hour and 15 minutes of cooking. Kabocha, calabaza, or butternut squash all work well, and the soup gets its body from the puréed squash, so there is no need for cream or butter.

| Ingredient | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Kabocha, calabaza, or butternut squash, peeled and cubed | 3 pounds (about 8 cups) |
| Water or low sodium vegetable broth | 10 cups, divided |
| Olive oil | 2 tablespoons |
| Haitian epis | 1/2 cup |
| Yellow onion, chopped | 1 large |
| Garlic, minced | 4 cloves |
| Celery, sliced | 2 stalks |
| Leek, white and light green parts, sliced | 1 medium |
| Carrots, sliced into rounds | 3 medium |
| Potatoes, peeled and cubed | 2 medium |
| Turnip or malanga, peeled and cubed | 1 medium |
| Green cabbage, thinly sliced | 1/2 small head (about 4 cups) |
| Cooked chickpeas, rinsed | 3 cups (or two 15 ounce cans) |
| Tomato paste | 2 tablespoons |
| Fresh thyme | 6 sprigs |
| Fresh parsley, chopped | 1/2 cup |
| Whole cloves | 3 |
| Whole scotch bonnet pepper | 1, left whole |
| Rigatoni, penne, or spaghetti broken into pieces | 8 ounces |
| Fresh lime juice | 2 tablespoons |
| Salt and black pepper | To taste |

- Squash : Simmer cubed squash until very soft
- Purée : Blend squash with its cooking water until smooth
- Base : Sauté epis, onion, garlic, and tomato paste
- Simmer : Add broth, vegetables, chickpeas, and herbs
- Finish : Add pasta and cabbage, then lime and salt

### Step 1: Cook and purée the squash

Place the cubed squash in a large pot with 4 cups of the water or broth. Bring it to a boil, then lower the heat and simmer, covered, for about 20 to 25 minutes, until a fork slides through the squash with no resistance. Carefully blend the squash and its cooking liquid until completely smooth, using a blender in batches or an immersion blender right in the pot. For the silkiest texture, press the purée through a fine strainer, as some Haitian cooks do.

### Step 2: Build the flavor base

In a large soup pot, warm the olive oil over medium heat. Add the epis, onion, garlic, celery, and leek, and cook for about 5 minutes, stirring often, until fragrant and soft. Stir in the tomato paste and cook for another minute or two so it darkens slightly and loses its raw taste.

### Step 3: Simmer the vegetables and chickpeas

Pour the squash purée into the pot along with the remaining 6 cups of water or broth. Add the carrots, potatoes, turnip or malanga, chickpeas, thyme, cloves, and the whole scotch bonnet pepper. Bring to a gentle boil, then reduce the heat and simmer for about 25 minutes, stirring now and then, until the potatoes and carrots are tender. Keep the pepper whole so it adds flavor and gentle warmth without making the soup too spicy, and remove it before serving.

### Step 4: Add the cabbage and pasta

Stir in the cabbage and the pasta and simmer for another 12 to 15 minutes, until the pasta is tender and the cabbage is soft. If the soup becomes too thick, add hot water a half cup at a time. Remove the thyme stems, the cloves if you can find them, and the scotch bonnet. Stir in the parsley and lime juice, then taste and season with salt and black pepper.

## Tips, substitutions, and storage

The quality of your squash makes the biggest difference. A deeply orange kabocha or calabaza gives a richer color and sweeter flavor than a pale squash. If your epis already contains salt or bouillon, add salt slowly at the end so the soup does not become too salty. Choose a low sodium broth whenever you can, because soups can carry a lot of hidden salt.

For extra protein, you can add white beans along with the chickpeas, and for a gluten free version use a gluten free pasta and cook it separately so it does not break apart. Plantain or yam can replace the potatoes for a more traditional touch. If you do not have epis on hand, blend a handful of parsley, a few scallions, a green bell pepper, garlic, thyme leaves, a little oil, and a squeeze of lime, and you will have a simple version in minutes.

**Make ahead tips**
- Cook and purée the squash a day early
- Keep pasta separate if storing leftovers
- Add a splash of water when reheating
- Freeze the soup without pasta for best texture

The pasta keeps absorbing broth as it sits, so if you plan to have leftovers, cook the pasta separately and add it to each bowl. FoodSafety.gov advises that vegetable soups and stews keep for 3 to 4 days in the refrigerator and 2 to 3 months in the freezer, and that leftovers should be reheated to 165°F. The soup often tastes even better the next day, which makes it a wonderful dish to cook on Friday for the Sabbath.

## Questions people ask

### Why do Haitians eat soup joumou on January 1?

Haitians eat soup joumou on January 1 to celebrate Haiti's independence, which was proclaimed on January 1, 1804, in Gonaïves. Under French colonial rule the soup was reserved for slave owners, and enslaved Haitians prepared it but were never allowed to eat it themselves. After independence, Haitians claimed the very soup that had been denied to them, and it became a symbol of freedom and dignity. Every New Year's Day, families share it to remember the revolution and the courage of those who came before them.

### Is soup joumou only eaten on New Year's Day?

Soup joumou is best known as the first meal of the new year, but it is not only a New Year's Day dish. UNESCO notes that it is also a traditional Sunday breakfast in Haiti. Many families continue serving it on January 2, Ancestry Day, a holiday honoring the heroes of independence. Because it tastes even better the next day, it is also a wonderful soup to cook on Friday for the Sabbath.

### What kind of squash is used for soup joumou?

Soup joumou is made with a bright orange squash, and kabocha, calabaza, or butternut squash all work well in this plant based recipe. UNESCO lists giraumon pumpkin among the traditional ingredients of the soup. A deeply orange kabocha or calabaza gives a richer color and a sweeter flavor than a pale squash. The squash is simmered until very soft and then puréed, which gives the soup its body without any cream or butter.

### How long does soup joumou last in the fridge?

Soup joumou keeps for 3 to 4 days in the refrigerator, according to FoodSafety.gov guidance for vegetable soups and stews. It can also be frozen for 2 to 3 months, and it freezes best without the pasta. Because pasta keeps absorbing broth as it sits, cook it separately if you plan to have leftovers and add it to each bowl. Reheat leftovers to 165°F, adding a splash of water if the soup has thickened.

## Reflection questions

Spend a few minutes with these questions, perhaps while the soup simmers or around the table with your family. What does freedom mean to you, both the freedom our ancestors fought for and the freedom Jesus offers? Is there an area of your life where you still feel bound, and what would it look like to bring it to Christ? And how could you use a family tradition like soup joumou to tell the next generation about God's faithfulness?

## A word of encouragement

The story of soup joumou reminds us that what was once used to divide people can become a gift that brings them together. That is the story of the gospel too. Jesus takes what was broken and turns it into something that tells of His grace.

Whether this is your hundredth pot of soup joumou or your very first, cook it with gratitude. Share it with someone who needs a warm meal or a kind word. And as you taste it, remember that the freedom Christ gives is for every person at the table.

## A prayer

Lord, thank You for the gift of freedom and for the courage of those who came before us. Thank You most of all for Jesus, who sets us free indeed. As we gather around the table, help us remember Your faithfulness and share Your love with everyone we meet. Break every chain that still holds us, and teach us to stand fast in the liberty You give. In Jesus' name, Amen.

## Your next step

If the story of freedom in this soup has stirred something in your heart, we would love to share more with you. Request a free Bible study and explore what Scripture teaches about the freedom Jesus offers, one on one, at your own pace. You are also warmly welcome to worship with us on Saturday morning in Alvarado, where we gather in Kreyòl and English and share a meal together after the Sabbath service.

# When Prayer Feels Quiet

URL: https://shekinahsda.org/blog/when-prayer-feels-quiet/
Category: Devotional
Author: Paul Edwards
Published: 2026-09-14

When prayer feels unanswered, the stories of Hannah, David, Elijah, and Daniel remind us that God's silence is not His absence and that He hears us from the very first day.


You have prayed about it for months, maybe for years, in the morning and again late at night. Still the diagnosis is the same, the job has not come, the relationship is still broken, and heaven seems strangely quiet. Somewhere along the way, a hard question has started to form in your heart: is God even listening to me?

If you have ever felt that way, you are in good company. Some of the most faithful people in the Bible prayed through long seasons of silence, weeping, questioning, and sometimes wanting to give up. God made sure their stories were written down, so that we would know we are not alone when prayer feels quiet.

In this article we will walk through the stories of Hannah, David, Elijah, and Daniel, and listen to what Jesus taught about praying without giving up. Our hope is not to offer easy answers. It is to help you keep talking to a God who has not stopped loving you, even when you cannot hear Him.

## The short answer

- 21 days : Daniel waited before the angel arrived
- 4 times : David asks "how long" in Psalm 13
- Always : Jesus said to pray and not to faint

The Bible never promises that every prayer will be answered quickly or in the way we hope. What it does promise is that God hears His children, that He is working even when we cannot see it, and that silence is not the same as absence. Sometimes God says yes, sometimes He says no, and sometimes He says wait. The quiet seasons of prayer are often where trust grows deepest.

The Seventh-day Adventist Church's page on prayer is honest about this. It calls the times when God seems not to answer one of the hardest parts of prayer, and reminds us that His timing differs from ours. It describes God not as a vending machine but as a loving Father who builds character in every season.

## Why does God sometimes seem silent?

Many articles on this question focus mainly on what the person praying might be doing wrong. Scripture does teach that wrong motives (James 4:3), cherished sin, or broken relationships at home (1 Peter 3:7) can hinder prayer, and those are worth examining humbly. But it would be unbiblical to suggest that every quiet season is caused by something you did wrong.

The Bible points to other reasons too. "To every thing there is a season" (Ecclesiastes 3:1), and God may be answering in a way we do not yet recognize. Sometimes His answer is no, because like a good parent He knows what we ask would not be good for us. Jesus said, "your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him" (Matthew 6:8).

Scripture also pulls back the curtain on something we rarely consider: there is a real spiritual conflict happening beyond what we can see. The Seventh-day Adventist Church describes this in Fundamental Belief 8, The Great Controversy, as a cosmic conflict between Christ and Satan in which all of humanity is caught up. We will see that conflict clearly in the story of Daniel.

**What silence does not mean**
- It does not mean God has stopped loving you (Jeremiah 31:3)
- It does not mean your prayer was not heard (Daniel 10:12)
- It does not mean you lack enough faith to be heard
- It does not mean the story is over

## Hannah: pouring out a sorrowful heart

Hannah longed for a child, while her husband's other wife Peninnah had children and "provoked her sore, for to make her fret" (1 Samuel 1:6). This went on "year by year," and Hannah "wept, and did not eat" (1 Samuel 1:7). Her prayer was not one request answered the next morning but a sorrow she carried for years.

> "And she was in bitterness of soul, and prayed unto the LORD, and wept sore." 1 Samuel 1:10, KJV

Hannah prayed so intensely that the priest Eli thought she was drunk. Her reply is one of the most honest descriptions of prayer in the Bible: "I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit: I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but have poured out my soul before the LORD" (1 Samuel 1:15). She did not dress up her pain in polite words.

Something changed in Hannah before anything changed in her circumstances. She "went her way, and did eat, and her countenance was no more sad" (1 Samuel 1:18). Later she bore a son and named him Samuel, "Because I have asked him of the LORD" (1 Samuel 1:20). Her story shows that peace can come through prayer even while we still wait for the answer.

## David: asking "how long?"

Psalm 13 holds one of the most honest prayers in Scripture. David does not open with praise or polished language. He opens with a complaint many tired believers will recognize.

> "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me? How long shall I take counsel in my soul, having sorrow in my heart daily? how long shall mine enemy be exalted over me?" Psalm 13:1 to 2, KJV

Four times in two verses David asks "how long." He feels forgotten and tired of carrying sorrow every day, yet God chose to include this prayer in His Word. That tells us something important. Honest lament is not a lack of faith; it is a form of faith, because it keeps talking to God instead of walking away.

Then, with no sign that his situation has changed, David turns: "But I have trusted in thy mercy; my heart shall rejoice in thy salvation" (Psalm 13:5). His trust comes not from a sudden answer but from remembering who God is. When prayer feels quiet, we can follow the same path from honest questions to a decision to trust.

## Elijah: when you are too tired to go on

Elijah had just seen a great victory on Mount Carmel, yet soon after, threatened by Queen Jezebel, he ran for his life. Exhausted and afraid, he sat under a juniper tree and prayed, "It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers" (1 Kings 19:4). Even great faith can run out of strength.

God's first response was not a lecture but care. An angel touched Elijah and said, "Arise and eat" (1 Kings 19:5), and later came again, "because the journey is too great for thee" (1 Kings 19:7). Sometimes the most spiritual thing we can do in a dark season is to rest, eat, and let God care for our bodies before we try to understand everything.

At Mount Horeb, a great wind came, then an earthquake, then a fire, "but the LORD was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice" (1 Kings 19:12). Elijah also believed he was alone, but God told him of "seven thousand in Israel" who had remained faithful (1 Kings 19:18). God may be speaking more gently than we expect, and we may be less alone than we feel.

Related: [The Gift of Rest: Why Sleep Is Part of Our Worship](https://shekinahsda.org/blog/the-gift-of-rest-why-sleep-is-part-of-our-worship/)

## Daniel: heard from the first day

Daniel's story may offer the most surprising window into unanswered prayer. In Daniel 10, the prophet spent "three full weeks" mourning and fasting, eating "no pleasant bread" as he sought God for understanding (Daniel 10:2 to 3). For twenty one days, there seemed to be no response.

> "Fear not, Daniel: for from the first day that thou didst set thine heart to understand, and to chasten thyself before thy God, thy words were heard, and I am come for thy words. But the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me one and twenty days: but, lo, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me." Daniel 10:12 to 13, KJV

Daniel's prayer was heard on the very first day, and the delay was not God ignoring him. A real conflict was taking place in the unseen realm, and the messenger was withstood until Michael came to help. Adventists see here a glimpse of the great controversy, and many Adventist teachers identify Michael with Christ Himself.

We should not build more on this passage than it says, since the Bible does not tell us every delay has the same cause. But it does show clearly that a quiet heaven is not an inactive heaven. While Daniel waited, God was already moving, and the same may be true for you.

- Years: Hannah: She weeps and prays year after year before Samuel is born (1 Samuel 1:7 to 20).

- Daily sorrow: David: He asks "how long" and chooses to trust God's mercy (Psalm 13).

- Forty days: Elijah: Strengthened by food and rest, he travels to Horeb and hears a still small voice (1 Kings 19:8 to 12).

- Twenty one days: Daniel: His prayer is heard on the first day, while the answer is delayed by unseen conflict (Daniel 10:12 to 13).

## Jesus: pray and do not faint

Jesus knew His followers would face seasons when prayer felt unanswered, so He told a story for them. Luke states its purpose before the story begins. It is a word for every weary heart.

> "And he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint." Luke 18:1, KJV

In the parable, a widow keeps asking an unjust judge for justice, and he finally helps her simply because she will not stop (Luke 18:2 to 5). Then Jesus draws the contrast: "And shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him, though he bear long with them? I tell you that he will avenge them speedily" (Luke 18:7 to 8).

The point is that God is the opposite of the unjust judge. If an uncaring judge responds to persistence, how much more will a loving Father. Jesus ends by asking, "when the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth?" (Luke 18:8).

Jesus Himself prayed, "O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt" (Matthew 26:39). The cup did not pass, and through His suffering came our salvation. Paul prayed three times for his thorn to be removed and heard, "My grace is sufficient for thee" (2 Corinthians 12:9). Sometimes the answer is not a change in our circumstances but God's strength within them.

## How to keep praying when God feels silent

In a quiet season we also need practical ways to keep going. These steps are not a formula for answers. They simply keep the conversation with God open while you wait.

- Be honest : Tell God exactly how you feel, as Hannah and David did
- Care for yourself : Rest, eat, and let God restore you, as He did for Elijah
- Remember : Write down past times God has been faithful
- Keep asking : Follow Jesus' call to pray and not faint
- Do not wait alone : Share the burden with others who can pray with you

When your own words run dry, pray the Psalms, such as "Truly my soul waiteth upon God: from him cometh my salvation" (Psalm 62:1). When you do not know what to say, remember that "the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered" (Romans 8:26). Even a sigh can be a prayer.

It also helps not to carry the weight alone. At Shekinah in Alvarado, the church family meets for prayer on Zoom every Tuesday and Wednesday at 7:30 PM, and you can send a private prayer request through our website. When we cannot pray, others can hold us up until our voice returns.

## Questions people ask

### Does God hear every prayer?

The Bible teaches that God hears the prayers of His children, even when heaven seems quiet. When Daniel prayed for three full weeks with no visible response, the angel told him, "from the first day that thou didst set thine heart to understand, and to chasten thyself before thy God, thy words were heard" (Daniel 10:12). Jesus also said that our Father knows what we need before we ask Him (Matthew 6:8). Silence is not the same as absence, and a quiet heaven is not an inactive heaven.

### Why does God sometimes answer prayer with wait?

God sometimes answers prayer with wait because His timing is different from ours and He is often working in ways we cannot yet see. Ecclesiastes 3:1 reminds us that "to every thing there is a season," and the Seventh-day Adventist Church describes God as a loving Father who builds character in every season. Hannah prayed year after year before Samuel was born, yet she found peace while she was still waiting (1 Samuel 1:18). The quiet seasons of prayer are often where trust grows deepest.

### Is it wrong to question God when you pray?

It is not wrong to bring honest questions to God, because Scripture itself includes prayers like David's cry of "how long" in Psalm 13. David asked that question four times in two verses, and God chose to include his prayer in the Bible. Honest lament is not a lack of faith but a form of faith, because it keeps talking to God instead of walking away. Like David, we can move from honest questions to a decision to trust God's mercy (Psalm 13:5).

### What can I pray when I do not know what to say?

When you do not know what to say, you can pray the Psalms, such as "Truly my soul waiteth upon God: from him cometh my salvation" (Psalm 62:1). Romans 8:26 promises that the Spirit makes intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered. Even a sigh can be a prayer. You can also ask others to pray with you, and Shekinah Haitian Seventh-day Adventist Church in Alvarado, Texas, meets for prayer on Zoom every Tuesday and Wednesday at 7:30 PM.

## Reflection questions

Take some time with these questions, perhaps with a journal open. Which of these Bible stories feels closest to what you are experiencing right now, and why? What would it look like for you to pour out your heart honestly to God this week, without trying to sound strong? And what is one past answer to prayer you can write down and return to when the silence feels long?

## A word of encouragement

If prayer feels quiet for you today, please do not stop talking to God. Hannah was given peace before she was given a son, and David questioned and then chose to sing. Elijah was fed and rested before he heard the still small voice. Daniel was heard on the very first day, though he did not know it for three weeks.

You may not understand what God is doing right now, and that is all right, because faith only asks that we keep turning toward the One who loves us. "Weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning" (Psalm 30:5). Hold on to Him, and let Him hold on to you.

## A prayer

Father, sometimes my prayers feel like they disappear into the quiet. You know how long I have been asking, and You know how tired my heart is. Thank You that You heard me from the first day, even when I could not hear You. Give me the honesty of Hannah, the trust of David, the rest You gave Elijah, and the patience of Daniel. Help me keep praying and not lose heart, and let Your peace guard my heart while I wait. In Jesus' name, Amen.

## Your next step

You do not have to carry this alone. If something heavy is on your heart, send us a prayer request, and our church family will pray with you and for you. Share as much or as little as you like, and your request will be handled with care.

- Source: [Prayer, Seventh-day Adventist Church](https://www.adventist.org/prayer/)

- Source: [1 Samuel 1, Psalm 13, 1 Kings 19, Daniel 10, Luke 18 (KJV)](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=1%20Samuel%201%3A10-20%2C%20Psalm%2013%2C%201%20Kings%2019%3A4-12%2C%20Daniel%2010%3A12-13%2C%20Luke%2018%3A1-8&version=KJV)

- Source: [Daniel Chapter 10 (KJV)](https://www.kingjamesbibleonline.org/Daniel-Chapter-10/)

- Source: [Luke Chapter 18 (KJV)](https://www.kingjamesbibleonline.org/Luke-Chapter-18/)

- Source: [Why does God not answer my prayer?](https://altrincham.adventistchurch.org.uk/bibleinfo_questions/why-does-god-not-answer-my-prayer)

# Walk With Me: Starting a Sabbath Afternoon Walking Group

URL: https://shekinahsda.org/blog/walk-with-me-starting-a-sabbath-afternoon-walking-group/
Category: Health
Author: David Carter
Published: 2026-09-07

Walking is one of the simplest ways to care for the body God gave you, and a gentle Sabbath afternoon walk with others can turn exercise into fellowship and worship.


The Sabbath meal is finished, the plates are stacked, and the afternoon stretches out ahead like an open field. Some of the family are drifting toward the couch, the children are getting restless, and someone suggests a nap. Then another voice says, "Why don't we go for a walk?" It is such a simple idea, and yet that one question can turn a sleepy afternoon into one of the sweetest hours of the week.

Walking is the kind of exercise almost anyone can start. It needs no gym membership, no special skill, and very little equipment beyond a comfortable pair of shoes. When you walk with others, it becomes something more than exercise. It becomes conversation, friendship, and, on the Sabbath, a quiet way to enjoy the world God made.

This guide covers what health experts say about the benefits of walking and how much activity adults need. It also looks at what the Bible says about walking and nature on the Sabbath, and how a family, a group of friends, or a small church group can start a Sabbath afternoon walk. It is general health education, so if you have a medical condition or have not been active for a while, please check with your doctor before you begin.

## The short answer

- 150 minutes : Weekly moderate activity the CDC recommends for adults
- 30 minutes : One way to get there: 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week
- 60 minutes : Daily activity youth ages 6 to 17 need (HHS)

The CDC recommends that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity physical activity each week, and it names brisk walking as an example of moderate activity. You do not have to do it all at once. The CDC suggests that 30 minutes a day on five days a week is one simple way to reach the goal, and some physical activity is better than none.

Spiritually, a Sabbath afternoon walk fits beautifully with the purpose of the day. Jesus walked through fields with His disciples on the Sabbath, and Scripture invites us to see God's glory in creation. A gentle walk together, with conversation and gratitude, can be a restful way to honor the Lord of the Sabbath rather than a break from Him.

## The benefits of walking

Health organizations agree that walking is one of the most accessible forms of exercise there is. Mayo Clinic lists a wide range of benefits that come from regular walking. It can help you maintain a healthy weight, prevent or manage conditions such as heart disease, stroke, high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, and some cancers, improve heart health and endurance, and strengthen bones and muscles.

Mayo Clinic also notes that walking can boost energy, improve mood, thinking, memory, and sleep, and reduce stress and anxiety. For older adults, it can improve physical function and lower the risk of falls. The American Heart Association likewise says walking can have a significant impact on your health by lowering your chances of heart disease. The Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans add that some benefits come right away, since physical activity has immediate benefits such as reducing anxiety and blood pressure and improving the quality of sleep.

**What regular walking can do**
- Support a healthy weight
- Lower the risk of heart disease, stroke, and type 2 diabetes
- Strengthen bones and muscles
- Lift mood and reduce stress
- Improve sleep and energy
- Help older adults lower fall risk

The guidelines also make a point that encourages beginners. The first key guideline for adults is simply to move more and sit less, and any amount of physical activity has some health benefits. If you have not exercised in years, you do not need to start at 150 minutes. A short walk after lunch counts, and so does every step you add from there.

## How much walking do you need?

The federal Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans recommend that adults get at least 150 to 300 minutes of moderate intensity aerobic activity each week. The CDC adds that adults also benefit from muscle strengthening activity on at least two days a week. For children and teens, the guidelines call for at least 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous activity every day for ages 6 through 17.

| Who | Weekly goal | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Adults | At least 150 minutes of moderate activity, such as brisk walking | CDC |
| Adults | Muscle strengthening at least 2 days a week | CDC |
| Youth ages 6 to 17 | At least 60 minutes of activity every day | HHS guidelines |
| Everyone | Move more and sit less; any amount helps | HHS guidelines |

How brisk is brisk? Harvard Health offers a simple talk test. Walk as if you are in a bit of a hurry, so that your breathing speeds up but you can still talk in full sentences. That pace is perfect for a group walk, because it keeps everyone moving while still leaving room for conversation.

## What the Bible says about walking

Walking is one of the Bible's favorite pictures of a life lived with God. Enoch is remembered in a single, unforgettable line: "And Enoch walked with God: and he was not; for God took him" (Genesis 5:24). To walk with someone is to share the same pace, direction, and company, which is a picture of friendship.

### God walked in the garden

The first walk in Scripture belongs to God Himself. After Adam and Eve sinned, they heard Him coming toward them in the evening. The moment is both sad and revealing.

> "And they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden in the cool of the day: and Adam and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the Lord God amongst the trees of the garden." Genesis 3:8, KJV

The first couple hid, yet the verse reveals something lovely about God's heart. The text suggests that walking in the garden in the cool of the day was a natural setting for God to meet with the people He made. Many readers have seen in this a glimpse of the fellowship God intended from the beginning, unhurried time together in the beauty of creation.

### Strength for the journey

Isaiah offers one of the most loved promises in all of Scripture. It was first spoken to God's people in a weary season. It still speaks to anyone who feels tired and worn down.

> "But they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint." Isaiah 40:31, KJV

The prophet is speaking about spiritual strength that comes from trusting God, not giving fitness advice. Still, the picture fits a walking group well. Each week you walk not only to strengthen your body but to remember that your deeper strength comes from waiting on the Lord.

## Is it okay to walk on the Sabbath?

This is a question many people ask, and it deserves a careful answer. The Bible does not list walking as forbidden on the Sabbath, and the Gospels show Jesus and His disciples walking through grain fields on the Sabbath day (Mark 2:23). When the religious leaders objected, Jesus said, "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath" (Mark 2:27). He also taught that "it is lawful to do well on the sabbath days" (Matthew 12:12).

The Seventh-day Adventist Church's Fundamental Belief 20 describes the Sabbath as "a day of delightful communion with God and one another" and "the day of rest, worship, and ministry." A quiet walk in nature with family and friends fits naturally within that picture. Spending part of the afternoon in nature also fits a day that celebrates God as Creator, since the Sabbath points us back to the world He made and called very good.

The key is the spirit of the walk. Training for a race, chasing a personal record, or turning the afternoon into a hard workout would shift the focus toward ordinary weekday goals. A Sabbath walk is different. It is gentle, unhurried, and centered on gratitude, fellowship, and the beauty of what God has made. If you are unsure where the line is for you, read Isaiah 58:13 prayerfully and talk it over with your family or a pastor.

> "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork." Psalm 19:1, KJV

Related: [Why Do Seventh-day Adventists Worship on Saturday?](https://shekinahsda.org/blog/why-do-seventh-day-adventists-worship-on-saturday/)

## How to start a Sabbath afternoon walking group

You do not need a committee or a budget to begin. A walking group can be as small as two friends or as large as a few families. What matters most is a simple plan, a welcoming spirit, and a little consistency.

- Invite : Ask two or three people after lunch
- Choose a route : Safe, well lit, and easy for everyone
- Set the pace : Walk at the speed of the slowest walker
- Add a moment of worship : A verse, a song, or a prayer
- Keep it going : Same time, same place, every week

### Start with a small circle

Begin by inviting a few people you already know, such as your family, a neighbor, or friends from church. Mayo Clinic suggests walking with a friend or neighbor or joining a walking group as a way to stay motivated. A small, faithful group often lasts longer than a large one that fizzles out.

### Pick a safe and pleasant route

Mayo Clinic advises walking in safe, well lit areas and avoiding the street or uneven, cracked sidewalks. For a Sabbath walk, look for a park, a quiet neighborhood, or a nature trail near where you live. Choose a loop that is easy to shorten, so that no one feels pressured to go farther than they can.

### Walk at the pace of the slowest walker

A Sabbath walk is not a race. Plan for the grandparent with a sore knee and the toddler who wants to look at every leaf. Harvard Health recommends warming up with five minutes of easy walking, and that fits a group perfectly. Let the first few minutes be slow and chatty, and let people who want a brisker pace walk a little ahead and circle back.

### Add a simple moment of worship

Before you start, read a short verse such as Psalm 19:1 or Isaiah 40:31 and say a brief prayer. Along the way, invite people to point out something in nature that reminds them of God's care. You might pause at the halfway point to share one thing each person is grateful for this week. These small habits keep the walk centered on the Lord of the Sabbath.

### Keep it simple and steady

Meet at the same time each week, perhaps right after the fellowship meal. Mayo Clinic encourages walkers to start with a small, achievable goal and to take missed days in stride, simply starting again when they can. If the group is ever tempted to grow into something more organized, check with your church leadership first so the effort can be planned and supported well.

## Practical tips for walking safely

Wear comfortable, supportive shoes that fit well. Harvard Health notes that sneakers are really all you need to get started, and Mayo Clinic recommends loose clothing suited to the weather. In North Texas, that usually means planning around the heat for much of the year, so bring water, choose shaded routes, and consider walking later in the afternoon when the sun is lower.

Mayo Clinic also suggests telling someone your route if you walk alone and wearing bright or reflective clothing if you will be out as it gets dark. Because the Sabbath ends at sunset, a late afternoon walk can finish with the sky turning gold, a beautiful time to close the day with prayer. If anyone in the group has heart disease, diabetes, joint problems, or another health condition, encourage them to talk with their doctor about what kind of activity is right for them.

## Walking together is a picture of the church

The Preacher in Ecclesiastes wrote, "Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up" (Ecclesiastes 4:9 to 10). Those words describe a walking group well, but they also describe the church. We were never meant to walk the Christian journey alone.

Think of the two disciples on the road to Emmaus after the crucifixion. Luke tells us that "while they communed together and reasoned, Jesus himself drew near, and went with them" (Luke 24:15). Some of the most meaningful conversations about faith happen side by side, on a path, with no rush to be anywhere else. Your Sabbath walk may become exactly that kind of place.

## Questions people ask

### How fast should I walk for it to count as exercise?

A walk counts as moderate exercise when it is brisk enough that your breathing speeds up but you can still talk in full sentences. Harvard Health calls this the talk test and suggests walking as if you are in a bit of a hurry. The CDC names brisk walking as an example of moderate intensity activity. That pace works well for a group, because everyone keeps moving while there is still room for conversation.

### Can I split my walking into shorter walks?

Yes, you can split your walking into shorter walks, because the CDC says you do not have to get all your activity at once. One simple way to reach the CDC goal of 150 minutes a week is to walk 30 minutes a day on five days a week. The Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans add that any amount of physical activity has some health benefits. A short walk after lunch counts, and so does every step you add from there.

### What do I need to start walking for exercise?

To start walking for exercise, all you really need is a pair of comfortable, supportive shoes that fit well. Harvard Health notes that sneakers are enough to get started, and Mayo Clinic recommends loose clothing suited to the weather. In North Texas, bring water and choose shaded routes during the hot months. If you have a health condition or have not been active for a while, check with your doctor before you begin.

### Is walking good for older adults?

Walking is very good for older adults, and Mayo Clinic says it can improve physical function and lower the risk of falls. Regular walking can also strengthen bones and muscles, lift mood, and improve sleep. For a group walk, warm up with five minutes of easy walking as Harvard Health recommends, and walk at the pace of the slowest walker. Anyone with heart disease, diabetes, joint problems, or another health condition should talk with their doctor about what kind of activity is right for them.

## Reflection questions

Consider these questions on your own or with the people you hope to walk with. Who in your life might be lonely on Sabbath afternoons and would be blessed by a simple invitation to walk? What would it look like for your family to spend part of the Sabbath enjoying creation instead of resting only indoors? How might walking alongside someone each week open the door to deeper conversations about faith?

## A word of encouragement

You do not have to be fit, organized, or outgoing to start something good. All it takes is one invitation and one afternoon. If only one other person says yes, that is a walking group.

As you walk, remember that the God who walked in the garden still delights in your company. He renews the strength of those who wait on Him, and He walks beside you on every path. Let each step be a small act of gratitude for the body, the friends, and the beautiful world He has given you.

## A prayer

Lord of the Sabbath, thank You for the gift of rest and for the beauty of everything You have made. Thank You for legs to walk, eyes to see Your handiwork, and friends to share the journey. Help us walk with You each day as Enoch did. Bless every step we take together, and draw near to us on the path just as You did on the road to Emmaus. Amen.

Join us on Saturday morning at 205 E Carver St in Alvarado, Texas, with Sabbath School at 10:00 AM and the Divine Service at 11:00 AM in Kreyòl and English, and stay for the meal our church family shares afterward. If a Sabbath afternoon walk sounds like something you would enjoy, the fellowship meal is a natural place to find a walking partner, so plan your first visit below.

# Diri ak Pwa the Healthy Way

URL: https://shekinahsda.org/blog/diri-ak-pwa-the-healthy-way/
Category: Recipes
Author: Rose Charles
Published: 2026-08-31

A full recipe for Haitian rice and beans made with brown rice, dry beans, and homemade epis, with simple nutrition and Scripture for everyday meals.


There is a certain sound every Haitian kitchen knows: the soft hiss of epis hitting hot oil, followed by the smell of garlic, thyme, and clove filling the whole house. Someone lifts the lid on a pot of beans, pours that deep red cooking liquid over the rice, and everyone knows dinner will be good. For many families, diri ak pwa is not just a side dish. It is the taste of home, of Sunday dinners, of grandmothers who never measured anything.

Now imagine that your doctor has suggested more fiber and fewer refined carbohydrates, or that you simply want your family to eat a little better. Your first worry might be that you will have to give up the rice and beans you love. The truth is the opposite. With brown rice, beans cooked from dry, and a homemade epis, diri ak pwa can become one of the most nourishing meals on your table while still tasting the way it should.

In this article we will walk through a full recipe for healthy Haitian rice and beans, show you how to make a simple plant based epis, and explain why beans and whole grains are so good for you. Along the way we will look at what the Bible says about everyday meals.

## The short answer

Healthy diri ak pwa uses three simple upgrades: brown rice instead of white, beans cooked from dry so you control the salt, and fresh epis instead of salty bouillon cubes. The method is the same one Haitian cooks have always used. You cook the beans, save their flavorful liquid, fry the beans briefly with epis, then cook the rice right in that liquid until every grain is tinted and tender.

- 6 : Servings from one pot
- 1 cup : Dry beans, about 2 1/2 cups cooked
- 30 min : Minimum boil for kidney beans

The dish many Haitians call diri kole ak pwa, or rice cooked together with beans, is a beloved everyday dish across Haiti and its diaspora. The classic version is usually made with red kidney beans, though many cooks use pinto or other beans too. Our version keeps the classic flavors of thyme, clove, garlic, and a whole scotch bonnet pepper, and simply makes the grain a whole grain.

## Why beans and brown rice are good for you

### What makes brown rice different

Every grain of rice starts as a whole kernel with three parts. The Mayo Clinic describes them simply: the bran is the hard outer coating that holds most of the fiber, the germ contains vitamins and healthy fats, and the endosperm is the starchy center. Brown rice keeps all three parts. White rice has the bran and germ removed, and with them most of the fiber.

Harvard's Nutrition Source reports that refining grains strips away much of their fiber, B vitamins, and vitamin E. It also points to research linking higher white rice intake with a greater risk of type 2 diabetes, and two or more servings of brown rice a week with a lower risk. Studies like these show associations, not guarantees, but they give good reason to choose whole grains more often. The Mayo Clinic adds that whole grains may help lower insulin levels and the risk of diabetes and heart disease.

### What beans bring to the table

Beans are one of the most humble and powerful foods in the world. Harvard describes legumes as a source of protein, fiber, folate, and iron, and notes that whole legumes are low in saturated fat and sodium. The Mayo Clinic adds that legumes contain no cholesterol and provide potassium and magnesium, and that they can stand in for meat. The USDA's MyPlate counts beans in both the protein group and the vegetable group, which says a lot about how useful they are.

Together, beans and brown rice make a filling plate full of fiber and plant protein. Add a slice of avocado and a fresh salad, and you have a complete Haitian meal that fits the plant based eating many Adventists enjoy.

Related: [Eating for Life: Simple Plant Based Meals from Our Kitchen](https://shekinahsda.org/blog/eating-for-life-simple-plant-based-meals-from-our-kitchen/)

## What the Bible says about everyday meals

### Eating to the glory of God

Paul wrote to the believers in Corinth about food, conscience, and how Christians should live together. He closed the discussion with a sentence that turns every ordinary meal into something sacred.

> "Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God." 1 Corinthians 10:31, KJV

In context, Paul was talking about food offered to idols and about caring for the conscience of others. But the principle is clear and broad. Nothing is too ordinary to be offered to God, not even a pot of rice and beans on a Tuesday night.

### Daniel's simple plate

When Daniel and his friends were taken captive to Babylon, they were offered rich food from the king's table. Daniel asked for something simpler.

> "Prove thy servants, I beseech thee, ten days; and let them give us pulse to eat, and water to drink." Daniel 1:12, KJV

The word "pulse" in the King James Version refers to food grown from seeds, which many Bible students understand to include vegetables, grains, and legumes. At the end of the trial, the Bible says, "at the end of ten days their countenances appeared fairer and fatter in flesh than all the children which did eat the portion of the king's meat" (Daniel 1:15). Scripture's main point is Daniel's faithfulness to God, not a diet plan, and we should be careful not to turn the story into a promise about weight or looks. Still, it is a beautiful picture of how simple foods, chosen with a faithful heart, were blessed by God.

## How to make a simple plant based epis

Epis is the flavor base of Haitian cooking, a blend of herbs, peppers, garlic, and onion that seasons everything from rice and beans to soups and stews. Many families keep a jar in the refrigerator at all times. Traditionally it is pounded by hand with a mortar and pestle, though most cooks today use a blender or food processor. This version makes about 1 1/2 cups.

| Epis ingredient | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Fresh parsley, stems and leaves | 1 packed cup |
| Scallions, roughly chopped | 4 |
| Green bell pepper, seeded and chopped | 1 medium |
| Small onion, chopped | 1 |
| Garlic | 8 cloves |
| Fresh thyme leaves | 1 tablespoon |
| Whole cloves | 2 |
| Fresh lime juice | 2 tablespoons |
| Olive oil | 1/3 cup |
| Scotch bonnet pepper, seeded | 1/4, optional |

Place everything in a blender or food processor and blend until you have a thick, bright green paste, scraping down the sides as needed. Add a tablespoon of water if it is too thick to move. Spoon it into a clean glass jar and refrigerate. Because homemade mixtures of fresh garlic and herbs in oil can carry a risk of botulism, Oregon State University Extension advises using them within 4 days, so freeze the rest in an ice cube tray and you will always have a few cubes ready for the next pot of beans.

## Diri ak pwa the healthy way: the recipe

This recipe serves 6. Plan to soak the beans overnight. Active time is about 30 minutes, cooking the beans takes about 1 hour to 1 1/2 hours, and the rice takes about 45 minutes plus a short rest.

| Ingredient | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Dry red kidney beans | 1 cup |
| Water for cooking the beans | 7 cups |
| Whole cloves | 4, divided |
| Long grain brown rice, rinsed | 2 cups |
| Olive oil | 2 tablespoons |
| Haitian epis | 1/3 cup |
| Garlic, minced | 3 cloves |
| Small onion, finely chopped | 1 |
| Fresh thyme | 4 sprigs |
| Whole scotch bonnet pepper | 1, left whole |
| Salt | 1 1/2 teaspoons, or to taste |
| Fresh parsley, chopped | 2 tablespoons, for serving |

- Soak : Soak the beans overnight, then rinse
- Boil : Cook beans until tender, saving the liquid
- Fry : Sauté epis, onion, garlic, and beans
- Simmer : Add rice, bean liquid, and herbs, then cover
- Rest : Let it steam 10 minutes, then fluff

### Step 1: Soak and cook the beans

Sort the beans, removing any shriveled ones or small stones, and rinse them well. Cover them with plenty of water and soak overnight in the refrigerator. The next day, drain and rinse the beans, then put them in a pot with 7 cups of fresh water and 2 of the cloves. Bring them to a full boil and keep them at a boil for at least 30 minutes, then lower the heat and simmer, partly covered, until the beans mash easily between your fingers. This usually takes 1 hour to 1 1/2 hours in total.

That boiling step matters. Raw or undercooked kidney beans contain a natural toxin, and Kansas State University food safety specialists advise boiling them in fresh water for at least 30 minutes and avoiding the slow cooker, which may not get hot enough. Wait to add salt until the rice step, because the Mayo Clinic notes that salt and acidic ingredients added early can toughen beans and slow their cooking.

### Step 2: Save the liquid and fry the beans

Strain the beans over a large bowl and save every drop of the cooking liquid, because it gives diri ak pwa its color and flavor. Measure the liquid and add water if needed to make 4 1/2 cups. In a heavy pot with a tight lid, warm the olive oil over medium heat and add the epis, onion, and garlic. Cook for 2 to 3 minutes until fragrant, then add the drained beans and stir for another 2 to 3 minutes so they soak up the seasoning.

### Step 3: Cook the rice

Add the rinsed brown rice and stir for a minute so every grain is coated. Pour in the 4 1/2 cups of bean liquid, then add the thyme, the remaining 2 cloves, the whole scotch bonnet, and the salt. Bring it to a boil and let it bubble uncovered for a few minutes, until the liquid drops just below the surface of the rice. Lower the heat as far as it will go, cover tightly, and cook for about 45 minutes without lifting the lid.

### Step 4: Rest and serve

Turn off the heat and let the pot rest, still covered, for 10 minutes so the rice finishes steaming. Remove the thyme stems, the cloves, and the scotch bonnet, and gently fluff the rice with a fork. Sprinkle with parsley and serve with sliced avocado, a green salad, steamed vegetables, or a spoonful of legim.

## Tips, substitutions, and storage

Brown rice can vary from brand to brand, so check it at 40 minutes. If the rice is still firm and the pot is dry, sprinkle in a quarter cup of hot water, cover, and cook a little longer. If you prefer the crispy layer at the bottom of the pot that many Haitians call graten, leave the pot on low for an extra few minutes, watching closely so it does not burn.

Pinto beans, black beans, or small red beans all work well in this recipe. If you are short on time, you can use two 15 ounce cans of beans, rinsed, and replace the bean liquid with low sodium vegetable broth, though the color will be lighter. Never use bouillon cubes without checking the label, since many contain animal products and a great deal of sodium.

**Keep it healthy and safe**
- Boil kidney beans hard for at least 30 minutes
- Add salt with the rice, not the beans
- Cool leftovers quickly and refrigerate
- Reheat leftovers to 165°F

Diri ak pwa keeps well in the refrigerator in a covered container for 3 to 4 days, and cooked beans freeze beautifully for later meals. Reheat leftovers until steaming hot, to 165°F as FoodSafety.gov recommends, adding a splash of water to loosen the rice. Making a big pot on Friday is a lovely way to prepare for the Sabbath, so your family can rest and still enjoy a warm, home cooked meal.

## Questions people ask

### Is Haitian rice and beans healthy?

Haitian rice and beans can be a very healthy meal when you use brown rice, beans cooked from dry, and fresh epis instead of salty bouillon cubes. Brown rice keeps the bran and germ, where most of the fiber lives, and Harvard's Nutrition Source links brown rice with a lower risk of type 2 diabetes. Beans add protein, fiber, folate, and iron while staying low in saturated fat and sodium. Together they make a filling plate of fiber and plant protein that fits the plant based eating many Seventh-day Adventists enjoy.

### What beans are used in diri ak pwa?

The classic diri ak pwa is usually made with red kidney beans, though many Haitian cooks use pinto or other beans too. Black beans and small red beans also work well in this recipe. If you use dry kidney beans, boil them in fresh water for at least 30 minutes, as Kansas State University food safety specialists advise, because raw or undercooked kidney beans contain a natural toxin. Save the cooking liquid, since it gives the rice its color and flavor.

### Can I use canned beans for diri ak pwa?

You can use canned beans for diri ak pwa when you are short on time, using two 15 ounce cans of beans, rinsed. Replace the bean cooking liquid with low sodium vegetable broth. The color of the rice will be lighter than the classic version made with beans cooked from dry. Check the label on any bouillon cubes before using them, since many contain animal products and a great deal of sodium.

### How long does diri ak pwa last in the fridge?

Diri ak pwa keeps well in a covered container in the refrigerator for 3 to 4 days. Cool leftovers quickly and refrigerate them, and cooked beans also freeze beautifully for later meals. When you reheat it, heat it until steaming hot, to 165°F as FoodSafety.gov recommends, adding a splash of water to loosen the rice. Making a big pot on Friday is a lovely way to prepare for the Sabbath.

## Reflection questions

Take a moment to think about these questions, on your own or with your family. Which everyday meal in your home could become a small act of worship if you offered it to God with gratitude? What might Daniel's quiet courage teach you about making faithful choices when everyone around you is doing something different? And who could you invite to share a plate of rice and beans this week?

## A word of encouragement

Healthy changes do not have to happen all at once. Maybe this week you try brown rice for the first time, and next month you make your own epis. Every small step taken with a willing heart honors the God who made you and loves you. The same Lord who blessed Daniel's simple meal is near to you at your own table, so cook with joy, eat with thanks, and trust Him with the rest.

## A prayer

Lord, thank You for daily bread and for the simple foods that grow from the earth. Thank You for the hands that taught us to cook and the families we gather with. Help us to eat, drink, and do everything for Your glory. Give us faithful hearts like Daniel's, and make every meal a reminder of Your goodness and care. In Jesus' name, Amen.

## Your next step

If you would like to learn more about the God who cares for every part of your life, we would be honored to study the Bible with you. Request a free Bible study and explore Scripture one on one, at your own pace. And if you live near Alvarado, come join us on a Saturday morning, when our church family worships in Kreyòl and English and shares a meal together after the Sabbath service.
